```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(broom)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(car)
library(lmtest)
library(emmeans)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
theme_gtsummary_compact()

# ---- fixed formatting helpers -------------------------------------------------
# Used so that every number quoted in the prose is generated from the fitted
# object, never typed by hand.
fmt   <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
# p-values so small that a rounded value is uninformative
fmt_psci <- function(p) {
  if (p < 1e-300) return("&lt; 1 &times; 10<sup>-300</sup>")
  e <- floor(log10(p)); m <- round(p / 10^e, 1)
  paste0(m, " &times; 10<sup>", e, "</sup>")
}
b  <- function(m, term, d = 4) fmt(coef(m)[term], d)
ci <- function(m, term, d = 4) {
  k <- confint(m)[term, ]
  paste0(fmt(k[1], d), " to ", fmt(k[2], d))
}
pv <- function(m, term) fmt_p(summary(m)$coefficients[term, 4])
```

```{r}
#| label: data

# Path is relative to this document: chapter/ sits alongside dataset/
mssm_raw <- read_excel(file.path("..", "dataset", "mssm_fasting_blood_sugar.xlsx"))

mssm <- mssm_raw |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    # Derived anthropometric indices
    bmi = weight_kg / (height_m^2),          # kg/m^2
    whr = waist_cm / hip_circum_cm,          # unitless ratio
    ruralurban = factor(ruralurban, levels = c("rural", "urban"),
                        labels = c("Rural", "Urban")),
    malefemale = factor(malefemale, levels = c("female", "male"),
                        labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    race       = factor(race, levels = c("malay", "chinese", "indian", "other"),
                        labels = c("Malay", "Chinese", "Indian", "Other")),
    marital    = factor(marital, levels = c("married", "single"),
                        labels = c("Married", "Single")),
    hx_dm2     = factor(hx_dm2, levels = c("no", "yes"),
                        labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

# Variable labels used by every gtsummary table in the chapter
var_labels <- list(
  fasting_blood_sugar = "Fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)",
  age                 = "Age (years)",
  height_m            = "Height (m)",
  weight_kg           = "Weight (kg)",
  waist_cm            = "Waist circumference (cm)",
  neck_circum_cm      = "Neck circumference (cm)",
  hip_circum_cm       = "Hip circumference (cm)",
  bmi                 = "Body mass index (kg/m²)",
  whr                 = "Waist-hip ratio",
  sbp1                = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
  dbp1                = "Diastolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
  total_bilirubin     = "Total bilirubin (umol/L)",
  total_cholesterol   = "Total cholesterol (mmol/L)",
  fasting_tg          = "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)",
  ruralurban          = "Residence",
  malefemale          = "Sex",
  race                = "Ethnicity",
  marital             = "Marital status",
  hx_dm2              = "History of diabetes"
)

covariates <- c("age", "height_m", "weight_kg", "waist_cm", "neck_circum_cm",
                "hip_circum_cm", "bmi", "whr", "sbp1", "dbp1", "total_bilirubin",
                "total_cholesterol", "fasting_tg", "ruralurban", "malefemale",
                "race", "marital", "hx_dm2")

n_total <- nrow(mssm)
n_cov   <- length(covariates)
```

```{r}
#| label: models

# ---- simple linear regression: the two worked examples -----------------------
m_bmi <- lm(fasting_blood_sugar ~ bmi,     data = mssm)
m_mar <- lm(fasting_blood_sugar ~ marital, data = mssm)

# ---- the multivariable model that carries sections 5 to 8 --------------------
# Adiposity is represented by BMI and waist-hip ratio. Waist circumference is
# deliberately excluded: see the multicollinearity section, where the model
# containing all three is fitted to show what happens.
f_mlr <- fasting_blood_sugar ~ ruralurban + race + age + bmi + whr + sbp1 +
  total_cholesterol + fasting_tg + hx_dm2

m_mlr <- lm(f_mlr, data = mssm)

# reduced model for the general linear F-test (race, a 3 df block)
m_no_race <- lm(update(f_mlr, . ~ . - race), data = m_mlr$model)

# the same model with waist circumference added back, used only to demonstrate
# multicollinearity among three overlapping measures of adiposity
m_mlr_waist <- lm(update(f_mlr, . ~ . + waist_cm), data = mssm)

# ---- transformation models ---------------------------------------------------
m_log_tg  <- lm(update(f_mlr, . ~ . - fasting_tg + log2(fasting_tg)), data = mssm)
m_log_fbs <- lm(update(f_mlr, log(fasting_blood_sugar) ~ .), data = mssm)

# ---- interaction models ------------------------------------------------------
m_int_cat  <- lm(update(f_mlr, . ~ . + age:hx_dm2),     data = mssm)
m_int_cont <- lm(update(f_mlr, . ~ . + whr:fasting_tg), data = mssm)

# candidates examined for a numerical-by-numerical interaction, in the order
# they were specified before any were fitted
int_search <- tibble::tribble(
  ~pair,                          ~formula_term,
  "BMI x triglyceride",           "bmi:fasting_tg",
  "BMI x total cholesterol",      "bmi:total_cholesterol",
  "Waist-hip ratio x triglyceride", "whr:fasting_tg"
) |>
  mutate(res = map(formula_term, function(tm) {
    mi <- lm(update(f_mlr, as.formula(paste0(". ~ . + ", tm))), data = mssm)
    a  <- anova(m_mlr, mi)
    tibble(f = a$F[2], p = a$`Pr(>F)`[2])
  })) |>
  unnest(res)

n_mlr <- nobs(m_mlr)

# name R gives the interaction term (it orders factors as they appear)
tm_cont <- grep(":", names(coef(m_int_cont)), value = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers

# Diagnostic panels, built directly in ggplot2. performance::check_model() is
# deliberately avoided because the `see` package is not available here.
aug_of <- function(model) {
  broom::augment(model) |>
    mutate(.stdresid = rstandard(model))
}

p_resid_fit <- function(model, title = "Residuals vs fitted values") {
  aug_of(model) |>
    ggplot(aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 0.7) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Fitted value (mmol/L)", y = "Residual (mmol/L)", title = title)
}

p_qq <- function(model, title = "Normal probability plot of residuals") {
  aug_of(model) |>
    ggplot(aes(sample = .stdresid)) +
    stat_qq(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.7) +
    stat_qq_line(colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Standardised residual", title = title)
}

p_scale_loc <- function(model, title = "Scale-location plot") {
  aug_of(model) |>
    ggplot(aes(.fitted, sqrt(abs(.stdresid)))) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 0.7) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Fitted value (mmol/L)",
         y = expression(sqrt(abs("standardised residual"))), title = title)
}

# Residuals joined back onto the full dataset, so that they can be plotted
# against variables that are NOT in the model. lm() drops incomplete rows, so
# the join is made on the original row indices carried by the residual names.
resid_with_data <- function(model) {
  mssm |>
    mutate(.row = row_number()) |>
    inner_join(
      tibble(.row   = as.integer(names(residuals(model))),
             .resid = as.numeric(residuals(model))),
      by = ".row"
    )
}

p_resid_vs <- function(model, var, xlab, title = NULL) {
  resid_with_data(model) |>
    ggplot(aes(.data[[var]], .resid)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 0.7) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "Residual (mmol/L)", title = title)
}
```

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

A great deal of what health researchers measure is continuous. Blood pressure, body mass index, glycated haemoglobin, lung function, birth weight, serum cholesterol, quality-of-life scores, length of hospital stay — these are the quantities on which clinical decisions are made, populations are compared and interventions are judged. Linear regression is the standard method for analysing them, and it is the foundation on which almost every other regression model in health research is built.

## Why linear regression matters in health research

The appeal of linear regression begins with a limitation of simpler methods. A $t$-test can compare mean blood pressure between two groups, and a correlation coefficient can quantify the association between body mass index and blood pressure. Neither can answer the question that actually arises in practice: *how much* does blood pressure differ per unit of body mass index, among people who are otherwise similar in age, sex and physical activity? Linear regression answers precisely that. It expresses an association as an interpretable quantity in the units of the outcome, attaches a confidence interval to it, and adjusts it for other measured variables simultaneously.

That capacity for **adjustment** is what makes regression indispensable in epidemiology. Observational health data are confounded almost by definition: people who differ in one exposure differ in many others. A crude comparison of fasting blood sugar between urban and rural residents confuses residence with the age structure, diet, obesity and socioeconomic position of the two populations. Multiple linear regression estimates the difference associated with residence *among participants alike in the measured covariates*, which is the closest an observational analysis can come to the comparison a randomised trial would deliver. @sec-crude-adjusted of this chapter shows how consequential this can be, with an association that is highly significant before adjustment and entirely absent after it.

Linear regression matters for a second reason that has nothing to do with linear regression specifically. Logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression for counts, Cox regression for survival times and mixed-effects models for grouped data are all extensions of the same framework. The concepts developed here — the regression equation, the partial coefficient, adjustment, indicator variables, interaction, model diagnostics — transfer directly. A reader who understands linear regression thoroughly has already learned most of what the others require.

The final reason is professional rather than technical. Regression results dominate the medical literature, and they are frequently misreported. A survey of a full year of papers in the *BMJ*, *The Lancet* and the *New England Journal of Medicine* identified fifteen distinct categories of error in the use of correlation and regression, among them the omission of confidence intervals, over-reliance on $p$-values, and unclear reporting of sample size (Porter, 1999). Critically appraising such analyses is a core competency for a doctoral graduate in public health, and it requires knowing not only how the models are fitted but how they fail.

## Four use-cases in medicine, health and public health

### 1. Quantifying a dose–response relationship

The most direct use of linear regression is to express how much a continuous outcome changes per unit of a continuous exposure. Doll and colleagues (2002) modelled systolic and diastolic blood pressure against body mass index, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in 3,116 adults in the Seychelles and Switzerland, adjusting for age. Because the regression coefficient is a rate of change, their findings could be stated in directly usable terms: in men, an increase of 1.7 kg/m² in body mass index, or of 4.5 cm in waist circumference, corresponded to a rise of 1 mmHg in systolic blood pressure; in women the corresponding figures were 1.25 kg/m² and 2.5 cm.

This is regression doing what no dichotomised analysis can. Splitting body mass index into "obese" and "not obese" would discard the gradient entirely and reduce statistical power, a cost quantified by Altman and Royston (2006). The graded, continuous nature of the adiposity–blood pressure relationship was established in exactly this way by the Framingham investigators decades earlier (Kannel et al., 1967).

### 2. Adjusting for confounding in observational studies

The second use-case is adjustment, and its effects are often dramatic. Law and colleagues (2001) examined the relationship between size at birth and childhood blood pressure in 1,570 children aged three to six years across five countries. Blood pressure was positively related to the child's *current* weight, and it was only after regression adjustment for current weight and sex that the inverse association between birth weight and systolic pressure became clear: in Chile, adjusted systolic pressure rose by 4.9 mmHg (95% CI 2.1 to 7.7) for each kilogram *decrease* in birth weight.

Here adjustment did not merely refine an estimate — it revealed an association that the unadjusted analysis obscured. It also illustrates why adjustment demands subject-matter judgement rather than statistical routine, since whether current weight is a confounder or a variable on the causal pathway determines whether adjusting for it is appropriate at all. That distinction recurs throughout @sec-mlr.

### 3. Deriving reference values and prediction equations

Much of clinical medicine depends on knowing what is normal for a given patient, and reference standards are built by regression. The Global Lung Function Initiative derived spirometry reference equations from nearly 100,000 records on healthy non-smokers across 33 countries, modelling forced expiratory volume and forced vital capacity as continuous functions of age, height, sex and ethnicity (Quanjer et al., 2012). The resulting equations, and the lower limits of normal derived from them, are now the international standard for interpreting a spirometry result.

The same approach underlies the estimation of kidney function. The CKD-EPI equation was developed by regressing log-transformed measured glomerular filtration rate on serum creatinine, age, sex and race in 8,254 participants, then validating it in an independent sample of 3,896 (Levey et al., 2009). Every laboratory report of an estimated GFR is the output of a fitted regression equation. Note in both examples the use of a logarithmic transformation of the outcome, the technique developed in @sec-transformation.

### 4. Evaluating interventions on a continuous endpoint

The fourth use-case is the analysis of trials and programme evaluations whose endpoint is continuous. The DASH trial randomised 459 adults to a control diet, a fruit-and-vegetable diet, or a combination diet, holding sodium intake and body weight constant (Appel et al., 1997). The combination diet lowered systolic blood pressure by 5.5 mmHg and diastolic by 3.0 mmHg more than the control diet, with substantially larger effects of 11.4 and 5.5 mmHg among participants with hypertension.

Randomisation removes confounding, so why use regression at all? Because adjusting the follow-up measurement for its own baseline value increases precision considerably, and because analysis of covariance — regression of the follow-up outcome on the baseline value plus the treatment indicator — is statistically preferable to comparing change scores or follow-up values alone (Vickers & Altman, 2001). The subgroup difference in the DASH results is also an instance of the phenomenon formalised in @sec-interaction: the effect of the intervention depended on baseline hypertension status.

## What this chapter covers

The chapter develops the method in the order in which it is used. @sec-slr introduces simple linear regression, least squares estimation, and the coefficient of determination with its many pitfalls. @sec-slr-assessment shows how to check whether a fitted model is trustworthy. @sec-mlr extends the model to several predictors, which brings adjustment, indicator variables and the general linear F-test. @sec-mlr-assessment applies the diagnostic machinery to the multivariable case and adds formal tests for normality and constant variance. @sec-transformation addresses what to do when the assumptions fail. @sec-interaction relaxes the assumption that a covariate's effect is the same for everyone.

Throughout, the same dataset is used and the same outcome is modelled, so that each technique is seen to build on the last. The analyses are real: where the data behave awkwardly, the awkwardness is reported rather than smoothed over, because recognising and handling such situations is the skill this chapter exists to teach.

# Simple Linear Regression {#sec-slr}

Regression analysis begins with the simplest useful case: one continuous outcome and one predictor. Almost everything that follows in this chapter — adjustment for confounding, diagnostic checking, transformation, interaction — is an extension of machinery that is easiest to see, and easiest to get wrong, in this two-variable setting. This section develops that machinery and applies it to a real survey dataset.

## The working dataset {#sec-data}

Every worked example in this chapter uses data from the **Metabolic Syndrome Study for Malaysia (MSSM)**, a community-based survey of adults. Each record is one adult participant. The survey collected sociodemographic information, anthropometric measurements, resting blood pressure, a panel of fasting venous blood investigations, and self-reported medical history. The dataset contains `r n_total` records.

The outcome variable throughout is **fasting blood sugar (FBS)**, measured in mmol/L. FBS is a natural teaching outcome for linear regression: it is continuous, it is clinically meaningful at the individual level, and it is the measurement on which the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus partly rests.

### Two derived covariates {#sec-derived}

Two of the covariates used in this chapter are not measured directly but **derived** from measurements that are. Both are standard indices of adiposity in metabolic research, and each captures a different aspect of body habitus.

**Body mass index (BMI)** expresses weight relative to height and is a measure of *overall* adiposity:

$$
\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight in kilograms}}{(\text{height in metres})^2} \qquad \text{units: kg/m}^2
$$

**Waist–hip ratio (WHR)** compares abdominal with gluteofemoral girth and is a measure of *central* fat distribution:

$$
\text{WHR} = \frac{\text{waist circumference in cm}}{\text{hip circumference in cm}} \qquad \text{(unitless)}
$$

The distinction matters clinically. Two people with identical BMI may differ substantially in where that mass is carried, and central adiposity is the more strongly implicated in insulin resistance. Because the two indices measure different things, they are only weakly correlated with each other in these data ($r$ = `r fmt(cor(mssm$bmi, mssm$whr), 2)`), which means both can be entered into a model without difficulty. Both are, however, strongly related to waist circumference itself ($r$ = `r fmt(cor(mssm$bmi, mssm$waist_cm), 2)` for BMI and `r fmt(cor(mssm$whr, mssm$waist_cm), 2)` for WHR), a fact that becomes important in @sec-multicollinearity.

Deriving a variable does not exempt it from scrutiny. BMI here ranges from `r fmt(min(mssm$bmi), 1)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$bmi), 1)` kg/m², and WHR from `r fmt(min(mssm$whr), 2)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$whr), 2)`. The single WHR value above 1.5 is physiologically extreme and most likely reflects a measurement or recording error; it is reported here rather than silently removed, and its influence is assessed in @sec-assessing along with all other observations.

@tbl-descriptive describes the outcome and the `r n_cov` candidate covariates used in this chapter.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of participants in the MSSM dataset. Continuous variables are summarised as mean (SD) and median (IQR); categorical variables as n (%). The number of missing observations is reported for every variable."

mssm |>
  select(fasting_blood_sugar, all_of(covariates)) |>
  tbl_summary(
    label = var_labels,
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd}); {median} ({p25}-{p75})",
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
    ),
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 2,
    missing = "always",
    missing_text = "Missing"
  ) |>
  modify_header(label = "**Variable**", stat_0 = "**N = {N}**") |>
  as_gt() |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::pct(88))
```

Two features of @tbl-descriptive deserve attention before any model is fitted, because both shape the analysis later.

First, **the outcome is markedly skewed to the right**. The mean FBS of `r fmt(mean(mssm$fasting_blood_sugar), 2)` mmol/L exceeds the median of `r fmt(median(mssm$fasting_blood_sugar), 2)` mmol/L, and values extend to `r fmt(max(mssm$fasting_blood_sugar), 2)` mmol/L, giving a skewness coefficient of `r fmt(mean(scale(mssm$fasting_blood_sugar)^3), 2)`. This is not a data error. It is the expected shape for a glycaemic measurement in a general adult population: most participants cluster in a narrow normoglycaemic range, while a minority with impaired glucose regulation or established diabetes generate a long upper tail. This skew will have visible consequences in @sec-slr-assessment and @sec-mlr-assessment.

Second, **the data are almost complete**. The outcome is recorded for every one of the `r n_total` participants, as are age, sex, ethnicity, residence, all anthropometric measurements, blood pressure and fasting triglyceride. Only a few variables have any missing values at all, the largest among those used here being total bilirubin. All analyses use complete-case analysis, the default behaviour of the `lm()` function in R: any record missing the outcome or any covariate in a given model is excluded from that model. The sample size is therefore reported for every model fitted. With so little missingness the choice of missing-data method is inconsequential here, but that is a property of this dataset rather than a general licence — complete-case analysis is unbiased only when data are missing completely at random, and in datasets with substantial missingness that assumption deserves explicit examination.

## What simple linear regression is

Simple linear regression summarises the relationship between two continuous variables. One variable is treated as the **outcome**, and the other as the **predictor**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: simple linear regression

Simple linear regression is a statistical method for summarising and studying the relationship between two continuous variables, in which one variable, denoted $x$, is regarded as the **predictor**, **explanatory** or **independent** variable, and the other, denoted $y$, is regarded as the **response**, **outcome** or **dependent** variable.
:::

The method is called *simple* because it involves exactly one predictor. When two or more predictors are used, the method becomes multiple linear regression, the subject of @sec-mlr. Two points of vocabulary matter for the rest of the chapter.

The word **linear** refers to linearity in the *parameters*, not to a requirement that a scatter plot look like a straight line. A model containing $x^2$ or $\log x$ as a predictor is still a linear model, because the unknown parameters enter additively and are multiplied by known quantities. This is why the transformations in @sec-transformation remain within the linear regression framework rather than departing from it.

The word **regression** signals that the object being estimated is a *conditional mean*. Simple linear regression does not claim that FBS is a deterministic function of body mass index. It claims something weaker and far more useful: that the **average** FBS among people who share a given body mass index changes in a systematic way as that body mass index changes. Individual variation about that average is expected and is modelled explicitly.

The predictor need not be continuous. A binary predictor such as rural versus urban residence is entirely admissible, and @sec-slr-application works through such an example. What the *outcome* may be is more restricted: ordinary linear regression assumes a continuous outcome whose conditional distribution is approximately normal with constant variance. Binary and count outcomes require the related models named at the end of this chapter.

## The best fitting line

Suppose FBS is plotted against body mass index for every participant. Many straight lines could be drawn through the resulting cloud of points. The task is to choose one, which requires a definition of what makes a line good.

For a candidate line, the **prediction error** for participant $i$ is the vertical distance between the observed outcome and the value the line predicts:

$$
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
$$

where $y_i$ is the observed outcome and $\hat{y}_i$ is the predicted, or fitted, value. A natural objective is to make these errors collectively small. Simply summing them fails, because positive and negative errors cancel: a line lying far from every point can achieve a sum of zero. Two repairs are available — summing absolute errors, or summing squared errors.

The **method of least squares** takes the second option. It selects the values of the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of the squared prediction errors:

$$
Q = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - (b_0 + b_1 x_i) \right)^2
$$

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: the least squares line

The least squares line is the line $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$ for which the sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed outcomes and the fitted values is smaller than for any other line.
:::

Squaring rather than taking absolute values is partly a matter of mathematical convenience — the squared criterion is differentiable, and minimising it yields closed-form estimators:

$$
b_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2},
\qquad
b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}
$$

The second expression carries a useful geometric fact: **the least squares line always passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$**. It also has a statistical consequence worth remembering — because errors are squared, observations far from the bulk of the data influence the fitted line disproportionately. A single extreme observation can move the line appreciably, which is why the diagnostic work of @sec-slr-assessment is not optional.

Least squares is not the only estimation method. Maximum likelihood estimation is the alternative, and under the normal-error model described next the two coincide for the regression coefficients. Both yield estimators that are unbiased and, among linear unbiased estimators, have minimum variance.

## The simple linear regression model

The least squares line is a description of the sample. To generalise from the sample to the population — to construct confidence intervals and test hypotheses — a probability model is required.

::: {.callout-note}
## The simple linear regression model

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \ \text{independently}
$$

where, for the $i$-th observation:

- $y_i$ is the observed outcome;
- $x_i$ is the observed value of the predictor, treated as fixed and known;
- $\beta_0$ is the **population intercept**: the mean outcome when $x = 0$;
- $\beta_1$ is the **population slope**: the change in the mean outcome per one-unit increase in $x$;
- $\epsilon_i$ is the **error term**, unobservable, with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$.
:::

Taking expectations of both sides, and noting that $E\{\epsilon_i\} = 0$, gives the **regression function** — the equation for the conditional mean:

$$
E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i
$$

This equation is the object of inference. The line it describes is the **population regression line**, which connects the mean outcome of each subpopulation defined by a value of $x$. The sample estimates $b_0$ and $b_1$ estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$; a different sample would give somewhat different estimates, and none would reproduce the population line exactly.

The model asserts four conditions simultaneously. They are conveniently remembered by the mnemonic **LINE**, and each is checked in @sec-slr-assessment.

::: {.callout-note}
## The LINE conditions

| | Condition | Statement |
|:--|:--|:-----|
| **L** | **L**inear | The mean outcome is a linear function of $x$ |
| **I** | **I**ndependent | The errors are independent of one another |
| **N** | **N**ormal | The errors are normally distributed at each value of $x$ |
| **E** | **E**qual variance | The errors have the same variance $\sigma^2$ at every value of $x$ |

Equivalently: the errors $\epsilon_i$ are independent normal random variables with mean zero and constant variance $\sigma^2$.
:::

These conditions are not equally consequential. Tests and intervals are **very** sensitive to departures from independence, and **moderately** sensitive to unequal variances. Inference about $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ is comparatively **robust** to non-normality, particularly in large samples. Prediction intervals, by contrast, are quite sensitive to non-normality. This ordering matters when deciding which diagnostic failures demand action, and it is applied explicitly in @sec-mlr-assessment.

A notational convention is used throughout this chapter and is worth stating once. Greek letters ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, $\sigma^2$) denote unknown population parameters. Roman letters and hatted symbols ($b_0$, $b_1$, $\hat{\sigma}$) denote estimates computed from a sample. The fitted regression equation, which is what statistical software reports, is therefore

$$
\hat{y}_i = b_0 + b_1 x_i
$$

The error variance is estimated by the **mean squared error**, $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \sum e_i^2 / (n - 2)$, whose square root — the residual standard error — expresses the typical size of a prediction error in the units of the outcome. The divisor is $n - 2$ because two parameters have been estimated from the data.

## The coefficient of determination, $R^2$ {#sec-r2}

A fitted line has a slope, and the slope has a $p$-value. Neither answers a question clinicians and reviewers ask immediately: how much of the variation in the outcome does the predictor actually explain? The coefficient of determination answers exactly that, and it is built by partitioning variability.

Consider two ways of predicting a participant's FBS. Knowing nothing about the participant, the best available prediction is the overall mean $\bar{y}$. Knowing the participant's body mass index, the prediction becomes $\hat{y}_i$ from the fitted line. The total deviation of an observation from the overall mean decomposes exactly into the part the line explains and the part it does not:

$$
\underbrace{(y_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{explained by the line}} + \underbrace{(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}_{\text{left unexplained}}
$$

Remarkably, this identity survives squaring and summing over all observations, giving the fundamental partition of the sums of squares:

$$
\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SST} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SSR} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}_{SSE}
$$

$$
SST = SSR + SSE
$$

where $SST$ is the **total sum of squares**, $SSR$ the **regression** (explained) **sum of squares**, and $SSE$ the **error** (unexplained) **sum of squares**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: the coefficient of determination

$$
R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST}
$$

$R^2$ is the proportion of the total variation in the outcome that is explained by the regression on the predictor. It is bounded by $0 \le R^2 \le 1$, and is often reported as a percentage.
:::

### Calculating $R^2$ from the sums of squares

```{r}
#| label: r2-calc

av_bmi  <- anova(m_bmi)
ssr_bmi <- av_bmi$`Sum Sq`[1]
sse_bmi <- av_bmi$`Sum Sq`[2]
sst_bmi <- ssr_bmi + sse_bmi
r2_bmi  <- summary(m_bmi)$r.squared
```

It is worth assembling $R^2$ once by hand, so that the number reported by software is not merely accepted. For the regression of FBS on body mass index, the analysis of variance table gives

$$
SSR = `r fmt(ssr_bmi, 1)`, \qquad SSE = `r fmt(sse_bmi, 1)`
$$

so the total sum of squares is

$$
SST = SSR + SSE = `r fmt(ssr_bmi, 1)` + `r fmt(sse_bmi, 1)` = `r fmt(sst_bmi, 1)`
$$

and therefore

$$
R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{`r fmt(ssr_bmi, 1)`}{`r fmt(sst_bmi, 1)`} = `r fmt(r2_bmi, 4)`
$$

Body mass index explains `r fmt(100 * r2_bmi, 1)`% of the variation in fasting blood sugar in these data. Equivalently, `r fmt(100 * (1 - r2_bmi), 1)`% of that variation remains unexplained.

The **correlation coefficient** is closely related: $r = \pm\sqrt{R^2}$, taking the sign of the slope. Here the slope is positive, so $r = \sqrt{`r fmt(r2_bmi, 4)`} = `r fmt(sqrt(r2_bmi), 3)`$, which agrees with the directly computed Pearson correlation of `r fmt(cor(mssm$bmi, mssm$fasting_blood_sugar), 3)`. The two quantities carry the same information about strength of association, but they answer different questions: $r$ measures the strength and direction of linear association, while $R^2$ measures proportion of variation explained. Note also that $R^2 = `r fmt(r2_bmi, 4)`$ corresponds to $r = `r fmt(sqrt(r2_bmi), 3)`$ — squaring shrinks a modest correlation into a very small proportion of variance, which is why the two are so often misread against each other.

## Cautions in interpreting $R^2$ {#sec-r2-cautions}

$R^2$ is the most quoted and the most abused number in applied regression. Seven cautions apply, and several are illustrated directly by this chapter's own results.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Seven cautions in interpreting $R^2$

1. **$R^2$ and $r$ quantify only the strength of a *linear* relationship.** A perfect curved relationship can produce $r = 0$ and $R^2 = 0\%$. A small $R^2$ is therefore evidence against a *linear* association, not against association in general.
2. **A large $R^2$ does not mean the straight line fits well.** Another functional form may fit considerably better. This is the most common single misuse of $R^2$: a model can explain 90% of the variance and still show obvious curvature in its residuals. Only the diagnostics of @sec-slr-assessment can distinguish the two situations.
3. **$R^2$ and $r$ can be substantially altered by one or a few observations.** In small datasets, deleting a single point can move $r$ from strongly positive to strongly negative. Influence of this kind must be checked, not assumed absent.
4. **Association does not imply causation.** This caution turns on study design rather than on statistics. In an **experiment** the investigator sets the values of the predictor; in an **observational study** the investigator only records what occurred. Most regression analyses in health research, including every model in this chapter, use observational data, so causal language is not licensed by any value of $R^2$.
5. **Ecological correlations overstate the strength of individual-level association.** When the units of analysis are groups — districts, states, countries — and the variables are rates or averages, the resulting correlation is typically much larger than the corresponding correlation between individuals, because aggregation removes within-group variation. An analysis of aggregated data answers a question about groups, not about people.
6. **A statistically significant $R^2$ does not mean the slope is practically meaningful.** Large samples make it easy to reject the null hypothesis for a slope of negligible size. In these data body mass index explains only `r fmt(100 * r2_bmi, 1)`% of the variance in FBS, yet the slope is very far from zero in statistical terms ($p$ = `r fmt_psci(summary(m_bmi)$coefficients["bmi", 4])`) because `r fmt(nobs(m_bmi), 0)` participants contribute to the estimate.
7. **A large $R^2$ does not guarantee useful prediction.** Confidence intervals for the mean outcome, and especially prediction intervals for a new individual, may remain far too wide to be clinically actionable. Here the residual standard error is `r fmt(sigma(m_bmi), 2)` mmol/L — large relative to the range over which FBS is clinically interpreted.
:::

Two further points belong alongside these. First, there is **no universal threshold for a "large" $R^2$**: what counts as substantial depends entirely on the field. In laboratory measurement an $R^2$ of 30% might be unacceptable, whereas in population health research, where outcomes have many determinants, it may represent a strong finding. Second, **$R^2$ never decreases when a predictor is added**, even a predictor consisting of pure noise. Comparing models with different numbers of predictors therefore requires the **adjusted $R^2$**, which divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom; this is taken up in @sec-mlr.

The habit to carry into the applied work that follows is straightforward: **report the effect size with its confidence interval, let $R^2$ describe explanatory power, and never allow either to stand in for the other.**

## Application: fasting blood sugar and eighteen candidate covariates {#sec-slr-application}

The MSSM dataset provides `r n_cov` variables that are plausibly associated with fasting blood sugar, including the two derived indices of @sec-derived. A standard first step in a regression analysis is to examine each one separately against the outcome, fitting `r n_cov` simple linear regressions. This is sometimes called univariable or unadjusted screening, and its results are reported in @tbl-slr-all.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-slr-all
#| tbl-cap: "Eighteen separate simple linear regressions of fasting blood sugar (mmol/L) on each candidate covariate, ordered by the proportion of variance explained. Each row is a distinct model fitted to all records with complete data on the outcome and that covariate. For multi-category ethnicity no single slope exists, so the p-value is that of the overall F-test for the variable."

slr_one <- function(v) {
  m <- lm(reformulate(v, response = "fasting_blood_sugar"), data = mssm)
  g <- glance(m)
  tt <- tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
  is_block <- nrow(tt) > 1
  tibble(
    variable = as.character(var_labels[[v]]),
    type = if (is.numeric(mssm[[v]])) "Numerical" else "Categorical",
    contrast = if (is_block) "3 df block" else
      if (is.numeric(mssm[[v]])) "per 1 unit" else
        paste0(levels(mssm[[v]])[2], " vs ", levels(mssm[[v]])[1]),
    beta = if (is_block) NA_real_ else tt$estimate[1],
    lo   = if (is_block) NA_real_ else tt$conf.low[1],
    hi   = if (is_block) NA_real_ else tt$conf.high[1],
    p    = g$p.value,
    r2   = g$r.squared,
    n    = g$nobs
  )
}

slr_tab <- map_dfr(covariates, slr_one) |> arrange(desc(r2))

slr_tab |>
  mutate(
    est = if_else(is.na(beta), "—",
                  paste0(fmt(beta, 3), " (", fmt(lo, 3), " to ", fmt(hi, 3), ")")),
    p_fmt = if_else(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p, 3)),
    r2_fmt = fmt(100 * r2, 2)
  ) |>
  select(variable, type, contrast, est, p_fmt, r2_fmt, n) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Covariate", type = "Type", contrast = "Contrast",
             est = "b (95% CI)", p_fmt = "p-value",
             r2_fmt = "R² (%)", n = "n") |>
  cols_align("left", columns = c(variable, type, contrast)) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88))
```

```{r}
#| label: slr-notes
n_sig <- sum(slr_tab$p < 0.05)
r2_next <- max(slr_tab$r2[slr_tab$variable != "History of diabetes"])
```

@tbl-slr-all repays careful reading, and four lessons emerge.

**`r fmt(n_sig, 0)` of the `r n_cov` covariates are statistically significant, yet almost none explains much variance.** Setting aside history of diabetes, no covariate explains more than `r fmt(100 * r2_next, 1)`% of the variation in FBS. This is caution 6 of @sec-r2-cautions made concrete: with roughly `r fmt(round(median(slr_tab$n)/100)*100, 0)` observations per model, very small associations achieve very small $p$-values. A screening table of this kind identifies candidate variables; it does not rank their importance, and it certainly does not identify causes.

**History of diabetes stands apart.** It explains `r fmt(100 * slr_tab$r2[slr_tab$variable == "History of diabetes"], 1)`% of the variance in FBS — several times more than any other covariate. This is entirely expected and is a warning about interpretation rather than a finding: a self-reported diagnosis of diabetes is not a risk factor for high blood sugar but a consequence of previously measured high blood sugar. The variable is retained in the models that follow because it is a powerful predictor and because adjusting for it makes the remaining coefficients interpretable within diabetic and non-diabetic groups, but no causal reading of its coefficient is available.

**The two derived indices behave differently from each other.** Body mass index explains `r fmt(100 * slr_tab$r2[slr_tab$variable == "Body mass index (kg/m²)"], 2)`% of the variance and waist–hip ratio `r fmt(100 * slr_tab$r2[slr_tab$variable == "Waist-hip ratio"], 2)`%, both smaller than waist circumference alone at `r fmt(100 * slr_tab$r2[slr_tab$variable == "Waist circumference (cm)"], 2)`%. Deriving a variable does not automatically produce a better predictor: BMI discards information about fat distribution, and WHR discards information about overall size. Each is useful for what it measures, not because it is a composite.

**Two covariates show no evidence of association**: residence (`r fmt_p(slr_tab$p[slr_tab$variable == "Residence"])`) and sex (`r fmt_p(slr_tab$p[slr_tab$variable == "Sex"])`), with height marginal. Reporting these honestly is as much a part of the analysis as reporting the significant ones.

The remainder of this section examines two of these `r n_cov` models in full — one with a numerical predictor and one with a categorical predictor. **Body mass index** is chosen as the numerical example: it is a derived variable whose construction was set out in @sec-derived, it is universally understood in health research, and it reappears in the multivariable model of @sec-mlr. **Marital status** is chosen as the categorical example: it has two levels, which makes indicator coding easy to see, and it is significant with a very small effect — the clearest illustration in this dataset of the distinction between statistical and practical significance. These same two models are carried into @sec-slr-assessment for diagnostic checking.

### Worked example A: a numerical predictor {#sec-worked-numerical}

@fig-bmi-scatter shows FBS against body mass index with the least squares line superimposed, and @tbl-bmi reports the fitted model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Fasting blood sugar against body mass index in the MSSM dataset, with the least squares regression line and its 95% confidence band. The line summarises the conditional mean; the wide vertical scatter about it shows how much individual variation remains unexplained."

ggplot(mssm, aes(bmi, fasting_blood_sugar)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.16, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#C0392B", fill = "#C0392B", alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(x = "Body mass index (kg/m²)", y = "Fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi
#| tbl-cap: "Simple linear regression of fasting blood sugar (mmol/L) on body mass index (kg/m²)."

tbl_regression(m_bmi, label = list(bmi = "Body mass index (kg/m²)"),
               intercept = TRUE) |>
  add_glance_table(include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, nobs)) |>
  as_gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

The fitted regression equation is

$$
\widehat{\text{FBS}} = `r fmt(coef(m_bmi)[1], 3)` + `r fmt(coef(m_bmi)[2], 4)` \times \text{BMI}
$$

Each element has a direct reading:

- The **slope** is `r b(m_bmi, "bmi")` mmol/L per kg/m² (95% CI `r ci(m_bmi, "bmi")`). For every additional unit of body mass index, mean fasting blood sugar is higher by `r b(m_bmi, "bmi")` mmol/L. Because one unit of BMI is a small difference, a more communicable statement rescales it: a BMI higher by 5 kg/m² — roughly the gap between the middle of the normal range and the middle of the overweight range — corresponds to a mean FBS higher by `r fmt(5 * coef(m_bmi)["bmi"], 3)` mmol/L.
- The **intercept** is `r fmt(coef(m_bmi)[1], 3)` mmol/L, the estimated mean FBS at a body mass index of zero. This has no physical meaning. The intercept here is a mathematical anchor for the line, not a quantity to interpret, because $x = 0$ lies far outside the observed range of `r fmt(min(mssm$bmi), 1)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$bmi), 1)` kg/m². Centring the predictor on its mean would make the intercept interpretable as the mean FBS at average BMI.
- The **residual standard error** is `r fmt(sigma(m_bmi), 3)` mmol/L, so individual FBS values typically deviate from the fitted line by about that much — a reminder of how weak individual-level prediction is here despite a precisely estimated slope.

**Prediction** follows mechanically from the equation. Substituting a body mass index of 30 kg/m², the conventional threshold for obesity:

$$
\widehat{\text{FBS}} = `r fmt(coef(m_bmi)[1], 3)` + `r fmt(coef(m_bmi)[2], 4)` \times 30 = `r fmt(predict(m_bmi, data.frame(bmi = 30)), 3)` \ \text{mmol/L}
$$

This is an estimate of the **mean** FBS among people with a BMI of 30, not a prediction for any individual. Predicting an individual value requires a prediction interval, which is much wider than the confidence interval for the mean because it must also accommodate the residual variation of `r fmt(sigma(m_bmi), 2)` mmol/L. Note also that prediction is only defensible within the observed range of the predictor; extrapolating beyond it assumes the linear relationship continues where no data exist.

### Worked example B: a categorical predictor {#sec-worked-categorical}

When the predictor is categorical, the same algebra applies but the coefficients acquire a different meaning. Marital status has two levels, married and single. R codes it as an **indicator** (or dummy) variable taking the value 0 for the reference level, married, and 1 for single:

$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if participant } i \text{ is married} \\ 1 & \text{if participant } i \text{ is single} \end{cases}
$$

Substituting each value into the regression function shows what the two coefficients now represent:

$$
E\{\text{FBS} \mid \text{married}\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times 0 = \beta_0
$$
$$
E\{\text{FBS} \mid \text{single}\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times 1 = \beta_0 + \beta_1
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Interpreting an indicator variable

With a two-level categorical predictor, the **intercept is the mean outcome in the reference group**, and the **slope is the difference in mean outcome between the two groups**. Simple linear regression with a binary predictor is algebraically identical to a two-sample $t$-test assuming equal variances.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mar
#| tbl-cap: "Simple linear regression of fasting blood sugar (mmol/L) on marital status, with married as the reference category."

tbl_regression(m_mar, label = list(marital = "Marital status"), intercept = TRUE) |>
  add_glance_table(include = c(r.squared, sigma, nobs)) |>
  as_gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mar
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of fasting blood sugar by marital status. Box plots show the median and interquartile range; red points and intervals show the group means with 95% confidence intervals, which are the quantities the regression model estimates. The difference in means is real but small against the spread within each group."

ggplot(mssm |> filter(!is.na(marital)), aes(marital, fasting_blood_sugar)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4, outlier.alpha = 0.15, outlier.size = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, colour = "#C0392B", size = 0.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) +
  labs(x = "Marital status", y = "Fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)")
```

```{r}
#| label: mar-means
mar_means <- mssm |>
  filter(!is.na(marital)) |>
  group_by(marital) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(fasting_blood_sugar), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

The fitted equation is $\widehat{\text{FBS}} = `r fmt(coef(m_mar)[1], 3)` `r ifelse(coef(m_mar)[2] < 0, "-", "+")` `r fmt(abs(coef(m_mar)[2]), 3)` \times \text{single}$, and the coefficients recover the group means exactly:

- Mean FBS in **married** participants is the intercept, `r fmt(coef(m_mar)[1], 3)` mmol/L, which equals the directly computed married mean of `r fmt(mar_means$mean[mar_means$marital == "Married"], 3)` mmol/L.
- Mean FBS in **single** participants is $`r fmt(coef(m_mar)[1], 3)` `r ifelse(coef(m_mar)[2] < 0, "-", "+")` `r fmt(abs(coef(m_mar)[2]), 3)` = `r fmt(sum(coef(m_mar)), 3)`$ mmol/L, matching the directly computed single mean of `r fmt(mar_means$mean[mar_means$marital == "Single"], 3)` mmol/L.
- The **coefficient** of `r fmt(coef(m_mar)[2], 3)` mmol/L is therefore the mean difference, single minus married.

The 95% confidence interval for that difference is `r ci(m_mar, "maritalSingle", 3)` mmol/L and the $p$-value is `r fmt_p(summary(m_mar)$coefficients["maritalSingle", 4])`. The interval excludes zero, so there **is** evidence that mean fasting blood sugar differs by marital status: single participants average about `r fmt(abs(coef(m_mar)[2]), 2)` mmol/L lower than married participants.

This model is worth dwelling on, because it is the cleanest example in the dataset of a result that is statistically convincing and substantively slight. The $p$-value of `r fmt_p(summary(m_mar)$coefficients["maritalSingle", 4])` looks impressive; the $R^2$ of `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mar)$r.squared, 2)`% reveals that marital status accounts for about one part in `r fmt(round(1 / summary(m_mar)$r.squared), 0)` of the variation in FBS. A difference of `r fmt(abs(coef(m_mar)[2]), 2)` mmol/L is also small against a within-group standard deviation of roughly `r fmt(sigma(m_mar), 1)` mmol/L, as @fig-mar shows: the two distributions overlap almost completely.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A significant coefficient is not an important one

Marital status is significantly associated with fasting blood sugar ($p$ = `r fmt(summary(m_mar)$coefficients["maritalSingle", 4], 4)`) and explains `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mar)$r.squared, 2)`% of its variation. Both statements are true, and only the second one is informative about magnitude.

Note also that marital status is almost certainly a proxy here rather than a cause. Married participants in this sample are likely to be older, and age is itself associated with FBS. Whether the association survives adjustment for age is a question this simple model cannot answer — which is the motivation for @sec-mlr.
:::

Not every covariate produces even this much. Residence and sex, as @tbl-slr-all shows, give $p$-values of `r fmt_p(slr_tab$p[slr_tab$variable == "Residence"])` and `r fmt_p(slr_tab$p[slr_tab$variable == "Sex"])` respectively — no evidence of any difference in mean FBS. Such results should be reported as they stand. They do not demonstrate that the groups are identical; they show that any difference is too small to distinguish from zero at this sample size, with the confidence interval bounding how large it could plausibly be. Nor does a non-significant unadjusted result mean a variable is irrelevant to the analysis: residence is retained in the multivariable model of @sec-mlr, where its adjusted coefficient behaves differently from its crude one.

Both models are now fitted and interpreted. Neither has yet been checked. Coefficient tables of the kind shown above are the same whether the model's assumptions hold or fail completely, which is why the next section examines the residuals before any of these conclusions is allowed to stand.

# Assessment of the Simple Linear Regression Model {#sec-slr-assessment}

The two models fitted in @sec-slr-application produced coefficient tables, confidence intervals and $p$-values. Those quantities are all computed under the LINE conditions. If the conditions fail, the arithmetic still runs and the table still prints, but the inference it supports may be wrong. Nothing in a coefficient table reveals whether this has happened.

Model assessment closes that gap. The strategy is indirect: the errors $\epsilon_i$ are unobservable, so their observable counterparts, the residuals, are examined instead. This section develops that examination and applies it to both worked examples.

## Residuals {#sec-residuals}

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: residual

The **residual** for observation $i$ is the difference between the observed and the fitted outcome:

$$
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
$$

It is the observable counterpart of the unobservable **error**, $\epsilon_i = Y_i - E\{Y_i\}$, which is the deviation of the observation from the *population* regression line.
:::

The distinction matters. The error measures distance from the true population line, which is never known. The residual measures distance from the fitted sample line, which is known. Residual analysis proceeds on the reasoning that if the model's conditions hold, the residuals should behave approximately as a sample of independent, normally distributed values with constant variance and mean zero.

Two properties of least squares residuals follow from the estimation itself and are not evidence of anything: they sum to zero, and they are uncorrelated with the predictor. Diagnostic information lies in their *pattern*, not their sum.

Because residuals are measured in the units of the outcome, judging whether one is "large" requires a scale. Dividing a residual by its estimated standard deviation gives a **standardised residual**, a unitless quantity expressing how many standard deviations an observation lies from the fitted line. This makes a rough flag available: standardised residuals beyond $\pm 2$ merit a look. That threshold should be used with care, since in well-behaved data roughly 5% of observations exceed it by chance alone; flagging only values beyond $\pm 3$, where about 0.2% would be expected, is often more practical. In either case a flagged observation is **marked for investigation, not for deletion**.

## Residuals versus fitted values {#sec-resid-fit}

The residuals-versus-fitted-values plot is the most frequently produced diagnostic in regression. Residuals are plotted on the vertical axis against fitted values on the horizontal axis. Because any observation lying exactly on the regression line has a residual of zero, the horizontal line at zero in this plot *is* the fitted regression line, viewed edge-on.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading a residuals versus fitted values plot

A well-behaved plot has three features:

1. Residuals **bounce randomly** about the zero line — supporting **linearity**.
2. Residuals form a **roughly horizontal band** of constant width — supporting **equal variances**.
3. **No residual stands out** conspicuously from the rest — suggesting no outliers.
:::

@fig-bmi-resid shows this plot for the regression of FBS on body mass index.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residuals versus fitted values for the regression of fasting blood sugar on body mass index. The red curve is a loess smoother. Two departures from the ideal are visible: the residuals are not a horizontal band of constant width but widen as the fitted values increase, and they are strongly asymmetric about zero, extending much further above the line than below it."

p_resid_fit(m_bmi, title = NULL)
```

The plot fails two of the three criteria. The vertical spread of residuals is far from constant: it is narrow at low fitted values and widens substantially as fitted values increase. And the residuals are strongly asymmetric, reaching almost `r fmt(max(residuals(m_bmi)), 0)` mmol/L above the line but only about `r fmt(abs(min(residuals(m_bmi))), 1)` mmol/L below it.

Both features are consequences of the outcome's skew, noted in @sec-data. Fasting blood sugar has a floor near zero but no practical ceiling, so participants with impaired glucose regulation generate large positive residuals with no negative counterparts. The equal-variance condition is not satisfied, and the normality condition is unlikely to be either.

A caution about reading such plots is warranted. Interpretation is subjective, and the temptation to see structure in randomness is strong — particularly in small datasets. The practical rule is that genuine problems announce themselves clearly; if a plot looks broadly acceptable, it usually is. The pattern in @fig-bmi-resid is not a subtle one.

## Residuals versus the predictor {#sec-resid-pred}

Residuals can also be plotted against a predictor. The criteria for reading the plot are exactly those of @sec-resid-fit, but its purpose depends on which predictor is chosen.

If the predictor is **already in the model**, the plot adds nothing in simple linear regression. Fitted values are a linear function of the single predictor, so this plot is a rescaled version of @fig-bmi-resid, horizontally stretched or reflected.

If the predictor is **not in the model**, the plot becomes genuinely informative, and this is where its value lies. Residuals may be regarded as a "new response" — the outcome after removing what the current model explains. Plotting this new response against a candidate predictor asks whether that variable explains any of the variation left over. A systematic trend indicates that it does and should be considered for inclusion; no trend indicates it need not be.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-resid-others
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the regression of fasting blood sugar on body mass index, plotted against two predictors omitted from that model. Both show a clear upward trend, indicating that age and fasting triglyceride explain variation in fasting blood sugar that body mass index alone leaves unexplained. This is direct diagnostic evidence for moving to a multivariable model."
#| fig-height: 3.6

p_resid_vs(m_bmi, "age", "Age (years)", "Residuals vs age") +
  p_resid_vs(m_bmi, "fasting_tg", "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)",
             "Residuals vs triglyceride")
```

@fig-bmi-resid-others makes the case for multiple regression on diagnostic grounds rather than by assertion. Both omitted predictors show clear upward trends against the residuals, so both explain variation that body mass index alone does not. This observation motivates @sec-mlr directly.

## Identifying specific problems from residual plots {#sec-resid-problems}

Different violations leave different signatures. @tbl-resid-patterns summarises the mapping.

::: {#tbl-resid-patterns}
| Pattern in the residual plot | Condition threatened | Typical remedy |
|:--------------|:---------|:------------|
| Residuals depart from zero **systematically** — for example positive at low $x$, negative at mid $x$, positive again at high $x$ | **Linearity**: the regression function is not linear | Transform the predictor; add a polynomial term; consider a more flexible model |
| **Fanning** — residuals tight at low fitted values, increasingly spread at high fitted values | **Equal variance** | Transform the outcome; use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors; use weighted least squares |
| **Funnelling** — residuals widely spread at low fitted values, tight at high fitted values | **Equal variance** | As above |
| A residual **stands apart** from the random pattern of the rest | An **outlier** is present, or the model is misspecified for that observation | Investigate the observation; check for measurement or data-entry error; assess its influence |
| Residuals show a **trend against a predictor not in the model** | An important predictor has been **omitted** | Add that predictor, or an appropriate transformation of it |
| Residuals show a **systematic pattern against time or spatial order** | **Independence** | Use a model for correlated data, such as a time-series model |

Mapping of residual plot patterns to the model condition they threaten.
:::

Two warnings apply to this table. First, a high $R^2$ provides no protection against any of these problems: a model can explain the great majority of the variance in the outcome and still display unmistakable curvature in its residuals. Second, more than one problem can occur simultaneously, and frequently does. In @fig-bmi-resid the same plot shows both non-constant variance and marked asymmetry.

## The normal probability plot of residuals {#sec-npp}

Equal variance and linearity are assessed from residual plots. Normality requires a different display: the **normal probability plot**, also called the quantile–quantile or QQ plot.

Its construction is a direct comparison of observed and expected quantiles. The residuals are ordered from smallest to largest. For each, the value that would be expected at that position in a sample of the same size from a normal distribution is computed. Observed values are plotted against expected values. Since the mean and variance of the errors are unknown, standardised residuals are used and the expected quantiles become standard normal scores. **If the residuals are normally distributed, the points fall approximately on a straight line.**

Four patterns recur, and recognising them is the point of the plot:

| Pattern in the normal probability plot | Interpretation |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|
| Points approximately on a straight line | Normality is reasonable |
| Straight except for one or two deviating points | Normality is reasonable apart from outliers, which should be investigated |
| A smooth curve, bending away from the line | The residual distribution is **skewed** |
| Straight in the middle, departing at both ends | The residual distribution is **heavy-tailed** |

```{r}
#| label: fig-bmi-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal probability plot of standardised residuals from the regression of fasting blood sugar on body mass index, with a histogram of the same residuals for comparison. The points track the reference line through the centre of the distribution but curve sharply upward in the upper tail, the classic signature of right skew. The histogram shows the same feature directly."
#| fig-height: 3.6

p_qq(m_bmi, title = "Normal probability plot") +
  (tibble(r = residuals(m_bmi)) |>
     ggplot(aes(r)) +
     geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey45") +
     labs(x = "Residual (mmol/L)", y = "Count", title = "Histogram of residuals"))
```

@fig-bmi-qq shows the third pattern unambiguously. The points follow the reference line through the central portion of the distribution and then curve steeply above it in the upper tail. The accompanying histogram confirms a long right tail. The residual distribution is skewed, not normal, with a skewness coefficient of `r fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_bmi))^3), 2)` — a symmetric distribution would give approximately zero.

How much this matters depends on what is being estimated, following the sensitivity ordering set out in @sec-slr. Inference about the slope is comparatively robust to non-normality, and at `r fmt(nobs(m_bmi), 0)` observations the central limit theorem protects the confidence interval for $b_1$ substantially. Prediction intervals for individual participants receive no such protection and would be unreliable here. The failure of equal variance seen in @fig-bmi-resid is the more serious of the two problems, because interval estimates and $p$-values are moderately sensitive to it.

## Further residual plot examples {#sec-resid-further}

Diagnostic plots look different when the predictor is categorical, and the second worked example illustrates this.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mar-resid
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic plots for the regression of fasting blood sugar on marital status. Because the predictor has only two levels, the model produces only two distinct fitted values, so the residuals fall into two vertical stripes of comparable length. The normal probability plot shows the same right skew as the previous model."
#| fig-height: 3.6

p_resid_fit(m_mar, title = "Residuals vs fitted values") +
  p_qq(m_mar, title = "Normal probability plot")
```

The left panel of @fig-mar-resid contains only two vertical stripes of points. This is not a defect: a two-level predictor generates exactly two fitted values, the two group means. The interpretive rules must be adapted accordingly. Curvature cannot be assessed at all, since two points always determine a straight line and the linearity condition is automatically satisfied for a binary predictor. What *can* be assessed is whether the two stripes have comparable vertical spread, which is the equal-variance condition in the form it takes here — the assumption of a two-sample $t$-test.

Here the two stripes are of similar length, and a formal test finds **no** evidence against constant variance ($p$ = `r fmt_p(bptest(m_mar)$p.value)`). This is an instructive contrast with @fig-bmi-resid. The equal-variance condition can hold comfortably in one model and fail badly in another fitted to the same outcome, because what the condition concerns is whether residual spread changes *across the fitted values* — and a two-level predictor produces only two of them. Passing this check is therefore much less reassuring for a binary predictor than it would be for a continuous one. The normal probability plot in the right panel still shows pronounced right skew, which is expected: the skew belongs to the outcome, and changing the predictor does not remove it.

For completeness, the patterns to expect in other situations are worth naming, since they will not appear in this chapter's data. A **correctly specified model** produces residuals of constant spread with no discernible pattern. A **wrongly specified functional form** produces curvature, often *together* with increasing variance, as two simultaneous problems. **Heavy-tailed errors** produce a normal probability plot that is straight in the middle and departs at both ends. And where curvature and non-constant variance occur together, transforming the outcome — for instance to $\sqrt{y}$ — can sometimes resolve both at once, with predictions then squared back onto the original scale. That remedy is the subject of @sec-transformation.

::: {.callout-important}
## Where this leaves the two simple models

Both models have markedly right-skewed residuals, and the body mass index model additionally has non-constant variance. The estimated slopes remain unbiased, and the substantive conclusions — a positive association with body mass index, a small negative difference for single participants — are unlikely to be artefacts. But for the body mass index model the standard errors, and therefore the confidence intervals and $p$-values, cannot be taken at face value.

Two responses are available, and both are pursued below: bring in additional predictors so that less variation is left unexplained (@sec-mlr), and transform the variables so that the conditions are better satisfied (@sec-transformation).
:::

# Multiple Linear Regression {#sec-mlr}

The diagnostic evidence of @sec-resid-pred showed that variables omitted from the simple model explain variation the model leaves behind. There is also a more fundamental reason to move beyond one predictor. In observational health research the association between an exposure and an outcome is almost never the association of interest on its own, because the people who differ in exposure differ in other ways as well. Multiple linear regression is the standard tool for separating these influences.

## From one predictor to several

Multiple linear regression extends simple linear regression to two or more predictors. The extension serves two distinct purposes, and confusing them is a frequent source of error.

The first is **prediction**. More predictors generally mean more of the outcome's variation is explained and individual predictions become more accurate.

The second, and in epidemiology far more important, is **adjustment**. Suppose interest lies in whether body mass index is associated with fasting blood sugar. Participants with a higher body mass index are on average older, have higher blood pressure and have higher triglyceride concentrations. The crude association of @sec-worked-numerical mixes all of these together. Multiple regression estimates the association attributable to body mass index *among participants who are alike in the other measured variables* — the **partial** or **adjusted** association.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The meaning, and the limits, of "holding other variables constant"

An adjusted coefficient is routinely described as the effect of a predictor "holding the other predictors constant". The phrase is accurate about the arithmetic and misleading about the science. It describes a *statistical* comparison between participants with identical values of the other predictors in the model. It does **not** mean the variable has been experimentally manipulated, and it does not extend to variables that were never measured. Adjustment removes confounding by the covariates in the model, and by nothing else.
:::

## The multiple linear regression model {#sec-mlr-model}

::: {.callout-note}
## The multiple linear regression model

With $k$ predictors,

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik} + \epsilon_i,
\qquad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \ \text{independently}
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the mean outcome when every predictor equals zero, and each $\beta_j$ is the change in the mean outcome per one-unit increase in $x_j$ **with all other predictors held constant**. The corresponding regression function is

$$
E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik}
$$
:::

Three points about this model deserve emphasis.

**"Linear" still refers to the parameters.** The predictors may include squares, logarithms or products of other predictors, and the model remains a linear model. This is what permits the transformations of @sec-transformation and the interaction terms of @sec-interaction to be handled without leaving the framework.

**The geometry generalises.** With one predictor the fitted model is a line; with two it is a plane; with more than two it is a hyperplane that cannot be visualised but is described by exactly the same algebra.

**The error variance estimate changes its divisor.** With $k$ predictors, $k+1$ parameters are estimated, so

$$
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \frac{SSE}{n - (k+1)}
$$

The sums-of-squares partition $SST = SSR + SSE$ carries over unchanged, and so does $R^2 = SSR/SST$, now called the **coefficient of multiple determination**. Because $R^2$ cannot decrease when a predictor is added, the **adjusted $R^2$** is used to compare models of different sizes:

$$
R^2_{adj} = 1 - \left( \frac{n-1}{n - (k+1)} \right) (1 - R^2)
$$

Unlike $R^2$, the adjusted version can fall when a predictor contributes less than its degree of freedom costs, which makes it the appropriate quantity for comparing competing models. It plays exactly that role in @sec-transformation.

### Categorical predictors and indicator variables

A categorical predictor with more than two levels cannot enter the model as a single number, because its codes carry no numerical meaning. It is represented instead by a set of **indicator** (dummy) variables: for a variable with $c$ levels, $c-1$ indicators are required, and the omitted level becomes the **reference** category.

Ethnicity in the MSSM dataset has four levels, so three indicators are needed. Taking Malay as the reference:

$$
x_{\text{Chinese}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Chinese} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\quad
x_{\text{Indian}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Indian} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\quad
x_{\text{Other}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Other} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$

A Malay participant has all three indicators equal to zero, so the reference category is absorbed into the intercept. Each of the three coefficients is then the difference in mean outcome between that ethnic group and the Malay group, adjusted for the remaining covariates. **The choice of reference category changes the coefficients but changes nothing substantive** — no fitted value, no $R^2$, and no overall test result depends on it. It is chosen for interpretability, and the largest or most clinically natural group is the usual choice.

## Fitting the multivariable model {#sec-mlr-fit}

The model carried through the remainder of this chapter regresses fasting blood sugar on nine covariates: place of residence, ethnicity, age, **body mass index**, **waist–hip ratio**, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, fasting triglyceride, and history of diabetes.

Adiposity is represented by the two derived indices of @sec-derived rather than by waist circumference. The reason is that waist circumference overlaps heavily with both — it is correlated `r fmt(cor(mssm$waist_cm, mssm$bmi), 2)` with body mass index and, being the numerator of the waist–hip ratio, `r fmt(cor(mssm$waist_cm, mssm$whr), 2)` with that. Entering all three would ask the model to separate three measurements of largely the same thing. @sec-multicollinearity fits exactly that model and shows what goes wrong. Using BMI and WHR together, by contrast, captures overall and central adiposity as two nearly independent dimensions.

@tbl-mlr reports the result.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mlr
#| tbl-cap: "Multiple linear regression of fasting blood sugar (mmol/L) on nine covariates, including body mass index and waist-hip ratio. Each coefficient is the estimated difference in mean fasting blood sugar per one-unit increase in that covariate, adjusted for all others in the model."

mlr_labels <- list(
  ruralurban = "Residence", race = "Ethnicity", age = "Age (years)",
  bmi = "Body mass index (kg/m²)", whr = "Waist-hip ratio",
  sbp1 = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
  total_cholesterol = "Total cholesterol (mmol/L)",
  fasting_tg = "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)",
  hx_dm2 = "History of diabetes")

tbl_regression(m_mlr, label = mlr_labels) |>
  add_glance_table(include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, nobs)) |>
  as_gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

The model was fitted to `r fmt(n_mlr, 0)` participants with complete data on all ten variables, `r fmt(n_total - n_mlr, 0)` records having been excluded. It explains $R^2 = `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$r.squared, 1)`$% of the variation in fasting blood sugar, with an adjusted $R^2$ of `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared, 1)`% — a substantial improvement on the `r fmt(100 * r2_bmi, 1)`% achieved by body mass index alone, and a direct vindication of the diagnostic signal in @fig-bmi-resid-others. The residual standard error has fallen from `r fmt(sigma(m_bmi), 2)` to `r fmt(sigma(m_mlr), 2)` mmol/L.

The fitted regression equation, written out in full, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{FBS}} = & `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)[1], 3)`
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["ruralurbanUrban"], 3)` \, (\text{urban})
`r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["raceChinese"], 3)` \, (\text{Chinese}) \\
& `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["raceIndian"], 3)` \, (\text{Indian})
`r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["raceOther"], 3)` \, (\text{Other})
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["age"], 4)` \, \text{age} \\
& + `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["bmi"], 4)` \, \text{BMI}
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["whr"], 4)` \, \text{WHR}
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["sbp1"], 4)` \, \text{SBP} \\
& + `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["total_cholesterol"], 3)` \, \text{cholesterol}
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["fasting_tg"], 3)` \, \text{triglyceride}
+ `r fmt(coef(m_mlr)["hx_dm2Yes"], 3)` \, (\text{diabetes history})
\end{aligned}
$$

Three coefficients illustrate how such a model is read.

**A continuous covariate.** The coefficient for fasting triglyceride is `r b(m_mlr, "fasting_tg", 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r ci(m_mlr, "fasting_tg", 3)`, $p$ `r pv(m_mlr, "fasting_tg")`). Among participants of the same residence, ethnicity, age, body mass index, waist–hip ratio, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol and diabetes history, a triglyceride concentration higher by 1 mmol/L is associated with a mean fasting blood sugar higher by `r b(m_mlr, "fasting_tg", 3)` mmol/L.

**A derived covariate on an awkward scale.** The coefficient for waist–hip ratio is `r b(m_mlr, "whr", 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r ci(m_mlr, "whr", 3)`, $p$ `r pv(m_mlr, "whr")`). Read literally this is the change in mean FBS for a one-unit increase in the ratio — but WHR spans only `r fmt(min(mssm$whr), 2)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$whr), 2)`, so a one-unit change is far larger than anything observed. A ratio is best rescaled before reporting: per 0.1 higher WHR, roughly the gap between the first and third quartiles of this sample, mean FBS differs by `r fmt(0.1 * coef(m_mlr)["whr"], 4)` mmol/L. **Whenever a coefficient's natural unit is much larger than the spread of the variable, rescale it before reporting.**

**A categorical covariate.** The coefficient for history of diabetes is `r b(m_mlr, "hx_dm2Yes", 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r ci(m_mlr, "hx_dm2Yes", 3)`). Adjusted for the other seven covariates, participants reporting a previous diagnosis of diabetes have a mean fasting blood sugar `r b(m_mlr, "hx_dm2Yes", 3)` mmol/L higher than those who do not. As noted in @sec-slr-application, this is a marker of established disease rather than a risk factor, and it is in the model to make the other coefficients interpretable rather than to be interpreted itself.

## Crude and adjusted estimates compared {#sec-crude-adjusted}

The purpose of adjustment is best seen by placing crude and adjusted estimates side by side, as in @tbl-crude-adj.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-crude-adj
#| tbl-cap: "Crude (unadjusted) and adjusted regression coefficients for fasting blood sugar. Crude estimates come from separate simple linear regressions, one per covariate; adjusted estimates come from the single multivariable model of @tbl-mlr. Adjustment attenuates every association, and for age it removes it entirely."

pretty_term <- c(
  "ruralurbanUrban" = "Urban vs rural residence",
  "raceChinese" = "Chinese vs Malay", "raceIndian" = "Indian vs Malay",
  "raceOther" = "Other vs Malay", "age" = "Age (per year)",
  "bmi" = "Body mass index (per kg/m²)",
  "whr" = "Waist-hip ratio (per unit)",
  "sbp1" = "Systolic BP (per mmHg)",
  "total_cholesterol" = "Total cholesterol (per mmol/L)",
  "fasting_tg" = "Fasting triglyceride (per mmol/L)",
  "hx_dm2Yes" = "History of diabetes (yes vs no)"
)

crude_tab <- map_dfr(
  c("ruralurban", "race", "age", "bmi", "whr", "sbp1",
    "total_cholesterol", "fasting_tg", "hx_dm2"),
  \(v) tidy(lm(reformulate(v, response = "fasting_blood_sugar"), data = mssm)) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    transmute(term, crude = estimate, crude_p = p.value)
)

adj_tab <- tidy(m_mlr) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  transmute(term, adj = estimate, adj_p = p.value)

left_join(crude_tab, adj_tab, by = "term") |>
  mutate(
    Covariate = pretty_term[term],
    `Crude b` = fmt(crude, 4),
    `Crude p` = if_else(crude_p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(crude_p, 3)),
    `Adjusted b` = fmt(adj, 4),
    `Adjusted p` = if_else(adj_p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(adj_p, 3)),
    `Change` = paste0(fmt(100 * (adj - crude) / crude, 0), "%")
  ) |>
  select(Covariate, `Crude b`, `Crude p`, `Adjusted b`, `Adjusted p`, Change) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88)) |>
  tab_footnote("Change is the percentage change in the coefficient from crude to adjusted.",
               locations = cells_column_labels(columns = Change))
```

Every association is attenuated by adjustment, which is the expected consequence of covariates that are correlated with one another and with the outcome.
