The attenuation is severe for the adiposity measures: body mass index falls from `r fmt(crude_tab$crude[crude_tab$term == "bmi"], 4)` to `r b(m_mlr, "bmi", 4)` mmol/L per kg/m², and waist–hip ratio from `r fmt(crude_tab$crude[crude_tab$term == "whr"], 3)` to `r b(m_mlr, "whr", 3)`, the latter losing statistical significance entirely ($p$ `r pv(m_mlr, "whr")`). Most of what the crude adiposity associations captured is shared with triglyceride, blood pressure and diabetes status — which is precisely what one would expect of the metabolic syndrome this study was designed to examine.

One result, however, is qualitatively different and is the most instructive finding in this chapter.

::: {.callout-important}
## Adjustment can eliminate an association entirely

Considered alone, age is strongly associated with fasting blood sugar: `r fmt(crude_tab$crude[crude_tab$term == "age"], 4)` mmol/L per year of age, with $p$ = `r fmt_psci(crude_tab$crude_p[crude_tab$term == "age"])`. It appeared in @tbl-slr-all as one of the more convincing covariates.

Adjusted for the other seven covariates, the age coefficient falls to `r b(m_mlr, "age", 4)` mmol/L per year with a 95% confidence interval of `r ci(m_mlr, "age", 4)` and $p$ = `r fmt_p(summary(m_mlr)$coefficients["age", 4])`. **The association has disappeared.**
:::

The explanation is not that age is unimportant, but that its crude association operates through the other measured variables. Older participants in this sample have a higher body mass index, higher systolic blood pressure and a much higher prevalence of diagnosed diabetes. Once participants are compared *within* strata of those variables, age itself adds essentially nothing.

Whether that is the right analysis depends entirely on the research question, and this is a subject-matter judgement rather than a statistical one:

- If the question is **how much fasting blood sugar differs between older and younger people in this population**, the crude estimate answers it, and adjusting away the pathways through which age acts would be a mistake.
- If the question is **whether age has an influence on glycaemia beyond its effects on adiposity, blood pressure and diabetes status**, the adjusted estimate answers it, and the answer is that it does not detectably.

The distinction is the classical one between confounders and mediators. A **confounder** is a common cause of exposure and outcome, and adjusting for it removes bias. A **mediator** lies on the causal pathway from exposure to outcome, and adjusting for it removes part of the very effect being estimated. The two are statistically indistinguishable — both change the coefficient when added to a model — and can be separated only by reasoning about the subject matter and the temporal ordering of the variables. Body mass index and diabetes status are far more plausibly consequences of ageing than causes of it, which suggests that here the adjusted age coefficient has removed mediated effects rather than confounding.

## Testing several parameters at once: the general linear F-test {#sec-f-test}

@tbl-mlr reports a $t$-test for each coefficient, each of which asks whether a *single* parameter is zero. Some questions cannot be phrased that way. Ethnicity occupies three coefficients, and "does ethnicity matter?" is a question about all three simultaneously. Testing them one at a time is both indirect and statistically wasteful, since performing several tests inflates the chance of a spurious result.

The **general linear F-test** answers such questions with a single test. Its logic is a comparison of two nested models:

1. Specify a **full model** containing all the parameters of interest.
2. Specify a **reduced model** obtained by imposing the constraint stated in the null hypothesis — here, that all three ethnicity coefficients are zero.
3. Compare the two models' error sums of squares.

::: {.callout-note}
## The general linear F-test

$$
F^* = \frac{\left( SSE(R) - SSE(F) \right) / \left( df_R - df_F \right)}{SSE(F) / df_F}
$$

where $SSE(R)$ and $SSE(F)$ are the error sums of squares of the reduced and full models, and $df_R$ and $df_F$ are their error degrees of freedom. The null hypothesis always corresponds to the **reduced** model and the alternative to the **full** model. A large $F^*$, and correspondingly small $p$-value, rejects the reduced model in favour of the full one.
:::

Because the reduced model is constrained, it can never fit better than the full model, so $SSE(R) \ge SSE(F)$ always. The test asks whether the improvement in fit is larger than the extra parameters would be expected to deliver by chance alone.

### Application: does ethnicity contribute to the model?

The hypotheses are

$$
H_0: \beta_{\text{Chinese}} = \beta_{\text{Indian}} = \beta_{\text{Other}} = 0
\qquad \text{versus} \qquad
H_A: \text{at least one is non-zero}
$$

```{r}
#| label: f-test
anova_race <- anova(m_no_race, m_mlr)
sse_r <- anova_race$RSS[1]; sse_f <- anova_race$RSS[2]
df_r  <- anova_race$Res.Df[1]; df_f <- anova_race$Res.Df[2]
f_race <- anova_race$F[2]
```

Fitting both models to the same `r fmt(n_mlr, 0)` participants gives $SSE(R) = `r fmt(sse_r, 1)`$ with $df_R = `r fmt(df_r, 0)`$, and $SSE(F) = `r fmt(sse_f, 1)`$ with $df_F = `r fmt(df_f, 0)`$. Substituting into the formula:

$$
F^* = \frac{(`r fmt(sse_r, 1)` - `r fmt(sse_f, 1)`) / (`r fmt(df_r, 0)` - `r fmt(df_f, 0)`)}
{`r fmt(sse_f, 1)` / `r fmt(df_f, 0)`}
= \frac{`r fmt((sse_r - sse_f) / (df_r - df_f), 1)`}{`r fmt(sse_f / df_f, 4)`}
= `r fmt(f_race, 2)`
$$

With `r fmt(df_r - df_f, 0)` and `r fmt(df_f, 0)` degrees of freedom this gives $p$ `r fmt_p(anova_race[["Pr(>F)"]][2])`. The reduced model is rejected: **ethnicity contributes to the explanation of fasting blood sugar after adjustment for the other seven covariates.**

This conclusion could not have been drawn safely from @tbl-mlr, where the Indian-versus-Malay contrast is not significant ($p$ = `r fmt_p(summary(m_mlr)$coefficients["raceIndian", 4])`) while the other two are. Individual contrasts answer questions about specific group comparisons; the F-test answers the question about the variable as a whole. The F-test is also invariant to the choice of reference category, whereas the individual $t$-tests are not — another reason to prefer it for this purpose.

Two special cases of the same test are worth recognising. When the reduced model contains only the intercept, the general linear F-test becomes the **overall F-test** reported with every regression output, testing whether all slopes are simultaneously zero; here it gives $F$ = `r fmt(summary(m_mlr)$fstatistic[1], 1)` on `r fmt(summary(m_mlr)$fstatistic[2], 0)` and `r fmt(summary(m_mlr)$fstatistic[3], 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ < 0.001. When the reduced model omits exactly one parameter, the F-test is algebraically equivalent to the $t$-test for that coefficient, since $t^2 = F$ on one numerator degree of freedom. The general form is needed only for testing a *subset* of two or more parameters.

## Multicollinearity {#sec-multicollinearity}

Adjustment relies on being able to separate the contributions of correlated predictors. When predictors are *highly* correlated with one another, that separation becomes unstable — a condition called **multicollinearity**. Its symptoms are inflated standard errors, coefficients that change substantially when a covariate is added or removed, and occasionally coefficients with implausible signs.

The **variance inflation factor** (VIF) quantifies it: $\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$, where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing predictor $j$ on all the others. A VIF of 1 indicates no correlation with the other predictors; values above 5 are commonly regarded as cause for concern and values above 10 as serious. For multi-category variables the generalised VIF is reported, and is compared after taking the root indicated by its degrees of freedom.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vif
#| tbl-cap: "Generalised variance inflation factors for the multivariable model of @tbl-mlr. All values are close to 1, so multicollinearity is not a concern in this model."

vif_names <- c(
  ruralurban = "Residence", race = "Ethnicity", age = "Age",
  bmi = "Body mass index", whr = "Waist-hip ratio",
  waist_cm = "Waist circumference", sbp1 = "Systolic blood pressure",
  total_cholesterol = "Total cholesterol", fasting_tg = "Fasting triglyceride",
  hx_dm2 = "History of diabetes"
)

vif_table <- function(model) {
  vm <- vif(model)
  tibble(
    Covariate = unname(vif_names[rownames(vm)]),
    GVIF      = fmt(vm[, "GVIF"], 2),
    Df        = as.integer(vm[, "Df"]),
    adj       = fmt(vm[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"], 2)
  ) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(adj = "GVIF^(1/(2·Df))") |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88))
}

vif_table(m_mlr)
```

@tbl-vif is reassuring: every value is close to 1, the largest being `r fmt(max(vif(m_mlr)[, 1]), 2)`. The nine covariates carry largely distinct information, and the adjusted coefficients can be interpreted without concern on this count. Body mass index and waist–hip ratio coexist comfortably because, as @sec-derived showed, they measure different things and are correlated only `r fmt(cor(mssm$bmi, mssm$whr), 2)`.

### What multicollinearity looks like when it is present {#sec-collinearity-demo}

This model was constructed to avoid the problem, and a reader could be forgiven for concluding that multicollinearity is a theoretical worry. It is not. The dataset makes it easy to demonstrate: simply add waist circumference back alongside body mass index and waist–hip ratio, so that three overlapping measures of adiposity compete to explain the same variation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vif-collinear
#| tbl-cap: "Generalised variance inflation factors after adding waist circumference to the model, so that three overlapping measures of adiposity are included together. Compare with @tbl-vif: the three adiposity terms are now badly inflated while every other covariate is unaffected."

vif_table(m_mlr_waist)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-collinear-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "The three adiposity coefficients estimated without and with waist circumference in the model. Adding a third overlapping measure roughly doubles the standard errors and renders all three terms non-significant, even though the model's explanatory power is unchanged."

adip <- function(model, terms) {
  tidy(model) |> filter(term %in% terms) |>
    transmute(term, est = estimate, se = std.error, p = p.value)
}
a1 <- adip(m_mlr, c("bmi", "whr"))
a2 <- adip(m_mlr_waist, c("bmi", "whr", "waist_cm"))

tibble(
  Term = c("Body mass index", "Waist-hip ratio", "Waist circumference"),
  `b (without waist)` = c(fmt(a1$est[a1$term == "bmi"], 4),
                          fmt(a1$est[a1$term == "whr"], 4), "—"),
  `SE (without waist)` = c(fmt(a1$se[a1$term == "bmi"], 4),
                           fmt(a1$se[a1$term == "whr"], 4), "—"),
  `p (without)` = c(fmt(a1$p[a1$term == "bmi"], 3),
                    fmt(a1$p[a1$term == "whr"], 3), "—"),
  `b (with waist)` = fmt(a2$est[match(c("bmi","whr","waist_cm"), a2$term)], 4),
  `SE (with waist)` = fmt(a2$se[match(c("bmi","whr","waist_cm"), a2$term)], 4),
  `p (with)` = fmt(a2$p[match(c("bmi","whr","waist_cm"), a2$term)], 3)
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(85))
```

```{r}
#| label: collinear-numbers
vif_waist <- vif(m_mlr_waist)[, 1]
se_ratio_bmi <- summary(m_mlr_waist)$coefficients["bmi", "Std. Error"] /
                summary(m_mlr)$coefficients["bmi", "Std. Error"]
anova_waist <- anova(m_mlr, m_mlr_waist)
```

The consequences are textbook, and every one of them is visible above.

**The variance inflation factors rise sharply, but only for the affected terms.** Waist circumference reaches `r fmt(vif_waist["waist_cm"], 1)`, body mass index `r fmt(vif_waist["bmi"], 1)` and waist–hip ratio `r fmt(vif_waist["whr"], 1)`, all beyond the conventional threshold of 5. Meanwhile residence, ethnicity, age, blood pressure, cholesterol, triglyceride and diabetes history are essentially unchanged from @tbl-vif. **Multicollinearity is a local problem**: it damages the estimates of the variables involved and leaves the rest of the model alone.

**The standard errors inflate.** The standard error of the body mass index coefficient increases by a factor of `r fmt(se_ratio_bmi, 2)` — the "variance inflation" the statistic is named for. This is the mechanism by which collinearity does its damage.

**Significance evaporates.** In @tbl-mlr body mass index was significant at $p$ `r pv(m_mlr, "bmi")`. With waist circumference added, all three adiposity terms become non-significant ($p$ = `r fmt(summary(m_mlr_waist)$coefficients["bmi", 4], 2)`, `r fmt(summary(m_mlr_waist)$coefficients["whr", 4], 2)` and `r fmt(summary(m_mlr_waist)$coefficients["waist_cm", 4], 2)`). A naive reading would conclude that adiposity is unrelated to fasting blood sugar, which is plainly false — the three measures are simply unable to be told apart.

**Yet the model as a whole fits no better.** The general linear F-test for adding waist circumference gives $F$ = `r fmt(anova_waist$F[2], 2)` on 1 and `r fmt(anova_waist$Res.Df[2], 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ = `r fmt(anova_waist[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 2)`, and the adjusted $R^2$ actually falls slightly, from `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared, 3)`% to `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr_waist)$adj.r.squared, 3)`%. Waist circumference contributes nothing that BMI and WHR have not already contributed; it merely makes the existing coefficients harder to estimate.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Recognising and handling multicollinearity

The signature is a combination that should always prompt suspicion: **a model that fits well overall while few or none of its individual predictors are significant**, often accompanied by coefficients that change substantially — sometimes reversing sign — when a covariate is added or removed.

Detection: inspect pairwise correlations among predictors before fitting, and compute the VIF afterwards. Values above 5 warrant attention, above 10 are serious. As a rule of thumb, avoid entering predictors correlated above about 0.7 into the same model; here waist circumference correlates `r fmt(cor(mssm$waist_cm, mssm$bmi), 2)` with BMI.

Remedies, in the order usually worth trying: **choose one measure from each correlated group** on subject-matter grounds, which is what @tbl-mlr does; **combine** the correlated variables into a single index, which is what BMI and WHR already are; or **centre** the predictors, which helps specifically for the collinearity between a variable and its own square or product term (@sec-interaction).

What multicollinearity does *not* do is bias the coefficients or damage the model's predictions. If prediction is the sole aim, it can be ignored. It matters when the goal is to interpret individual coefficients — which, in epidemiology, it usually is.
:::

The dataset offers other opportunities to create the same problem. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure are correlated `r fmt(cor(mssm$sbp1, mssm$dbp1), 2)`, and weight, hip circumference and neck circumference are all closely related to the adiposity measures already in the model. Entering several members of any of these groups together would reproduce the instability shown above.

The model is now fitted, its coefficients interpreted, its ethnicity block tested and its predictors checked for redundancy. What has not been examined is whether the conditions underlying all of these inferences are satisfied.

# Assessment of Multiple Linear Regression {#sec-mlr-assessment}

Every quantity in @tbl-mlr — each standard error, each confidence interval, each $p$-value, and the F-test of @sec-f-test — was computed on the assumption that the model's conditions hold. This section states those conditions for the multivariable case, assesses them graphically, and then applies the formal tests for the two that are most often examined in practice.

## The assumptions for multiple linear regression {#sec-mlr-assumptions}

The LINE conditions of @sec-slr carry over directly. The only change is that "at each value of $x$" becomes "at each **set** of values of the predictors".

::: {.callout-note}
## The LINE conditions for multiple linear regression

For each combination of predictor values $(x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ik})$:

| | Condition | Statement |
|:--|:--|:------|
| **L** | **L**inear | The mean outcome is a linear function of the predictors |
| **I** | **I**ndependent | The errors are independent of one another |
| **N** | **N**ormal | The errors are normally distributed |
| **E** | **E**qual variance | The errors have the same variance $\sigma^2$ |

Equivalently, the errors are independent $N(0, \sigma^2)$ random variables. Two further conditions are implicit: the predictor values are treated as **fixed and measured without error**, and the model is **correctly specified**, containing the variables that matter in the form in which they matter.
:::

A word on each condition as it applies to the model of @sec-mlr-fit.

**Linearity** is now a statement about each predictor's contribution, holding the others fixed. It could fail for one predictor while holding for the rest — for instance if fasting blood sugar rose with age up to a point and then levelled off. It is assessed one predictor at a time.

**Independence** requires that no observation's error conveys information about another's. It typically fails by design rather than by accident, in three recognisable situations: repeated measurements taken on the same individual over time; naturally grouped data, such as pupils within schools or patients within clinics, where members of a group resemble one another; and data collected in a time or spatial sequence, where neighbouring observations are correlated. None of these applies to the MSSM data, where each record is a separate participant measured once, so the condition is satisfied here. Where it does not hold, the remedy is not a repair to the linear model but a different class of model — mixed-effects models for grouped data, time-series models for sequential data. Independence deserves this attention because, as noted in @sec-slr, inference is *very* sensitive to its failure, and no residual plot will reveal a violation that the study design has built in.

**Normality** concerns the errors, not the outcome or the predictors. It is common to see the outcome's own distribution tested for normality before fitting a regression; this is not what the model requires. A markedly skewed outcome can still yield well-behaved residuals if the skew is explained by the predictors.

**Equal variance**, or homoscedasticity, requires the scatter of errors to be the same everywhere. Its failure does not bias the coefficients, but it invalidates the standard errors and therefore everything computed from them.

## Assessing the model assumptions {#sec-assessing}

All the diagnostic tools of @sec-slr-assessment apply unchanged. @fig-mlr-diagnostics shows the standard set for the multivariable model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mlr-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic plots for the multivariable model. Top left: residuals versus fitted values, showing a pronounced fan shape as fitted values increase. Top right: the normal probability plot, curving sharply upward in the right tail. Bottom left: the scale-location plot, whose rising smoother confirms that residual spread grows with the fitted value. Bottom right: histogram of residuals, showing the long right tail directly."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

(p_resid_fit(m_mlr, "Residuals vs fitted values") | p_qq(m_mlr, "Normal probability plot")) /
(p_scale_loc(m_mlr, "Scale-location") |
   (tibble(r = residuals(m_mlr)) |>
      ggplot(aes(r)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey45") +
      labs(x = "Residual (mmol/L)", y = "Count", title = "Histogram of residuals")))
```

The four panels tell a consistent story, and it is the same story as in @sec-slr-assessment.

The **residuals-versus-fitted plot** shows a clear fan: residual spread is narrow where fitted values are low and much wider where they are high. Equal variance fails. The **scale-location plot**, which plots the square root of the absolute standardised residual against the fitted value, makes the same point more directly — a horizontal smoother would indicate constant variance, and this one rises steadily. The **normal probability plot** follows the reference line through the centre and then departs sharply upward, the signature of right skew described in @sec-npp. The **histogram** confirms it: residual skewness is `r fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_mlr))^3), 2)` and kurtosis is `r fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_mlr))^4), 1)`, against values of 0 and 3 for a normal distribution.

Linearity is assessed predictor by predictor, in @fig-mlr-resid-preds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mlr-resid-preds
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the multivariable model plotted against each continuous predictor in the model. A horizontal smoother indicates that the predictor's linear specification is adequate. All six are close to horizontal across the bulk of the data, so the linearity condition is reasonably met for each; the wandering at the extremes of the triglyceride, cholesterol and waist-hip ratio panels reflects the sparse data there rather than systematic curvature."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

(p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "age", "Age (years)", "Age") |
 p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "bmi", "Body mass index (kg/m²)", "Body mass index") |
 p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "whr", "Waist-hip ratio", "Waist-hip ratio")) /
(p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "sbp1", "Systolic BP (mmHg)", "Systolic BP") |
 p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "total_cholesterol", "Total cholesterol (mmol/L)", "Cholesterol") |
 p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "fasting_tg", "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)", "Triglyceride"))
```

These panels are more encouraging. Each smoother is close to horizontal across the region where most of the data lie, so **the linear specification of each predictor is adequate**; the problems in this model concern the error distribution, not the functional form. This distinction matters for @sec-transformation, because it determines which transformation is worth attempting.

A final graphical check plots the residuals against predictors *omitted* from the model, asking whether an important variable has been left out.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mlr-omitted
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the multivariable model plotted against two measured variables omitted from it. Neither shows a strong trend, indicating that neither would add appreciably to the model — diastolic blood pressure because systolic pressure already carries that information, and waist circumference because body mass index and waist-hip ratio between them already do."
#| fig-height: 3.6

p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "dbp1", "Diastolic blood pressure (mmHg)", "Diastolic BP") +
  p_resid_vs(m_mlr, "waist_cm", "Waist circumference (cm)", "Waist circumference")
```

Neither omitted variable shows a marked trend in @fig-mlr-omitted, so neither is an obviously missing predictor. This is expected, since each is closely related to variables already included. The waist circumference panel is the graphical counterpart of the formal test in @sec-collinearity-demo: the flat smoother says there is no leftover signal for waist circumference to explain, which is why adding it inflated the standard errors without improving the fit.

### Outliers, leverage and influence

Three related but distinct ideas arise when individual observations are examined.

- An **outlier** has a large residual: its outcome is far from what the model predicts.
- A **high-leverage** point has an unusual combination of *predictor* values, far from the centre of the predictor space. Leverage concerns the $x$ values only and can be computed before the outcome is even seen.
- An **influential** point is one whose removal would materially change the fitted model. Influence combines the other two: a point that is both an outlier and high-leverage is the classic influential observation.

Conventional diagnostics and thresholds are as follows, with the values for this model shown.

```{r}
#| label: influence
n_obs   <- nobs(m_mlr)
k_pred  <- length(coef(m_mlr)) - 1
lev_cut <- (2 * k_pred + 2) / n_obs
cook_cut <- 4 / n_obs
n_lev   <- sum(hatvalues(m_mlr) > lev_cut)
n_cook  <- sum(cooks.distance(m_mlr) > cook_cut)
max_cook <- max(cooks.distance(m_mlr))
n_stdres <- sum(abs(rstandard(m_mlr)) > 2)
```

| Diagnostic | What it measures | Conventional threshold | This model |
|:-----|:------|:-----|:----|
| Standardised residual | How many SDs an observation lies from the fitted value | $\vert e^* \vert > 2$ (or $> 3$) | `r fmt(n_stdres, 0)` of `r fmt(n_obs, 0)` (`r fmt(100 * n_stdres / n_obs, 1)`%) |
| Leverage $h_{ii}$ | How unusual the predictor values are | $(2k+2)/n$ = `r fmt(lev_cut, 4)` | `r fmt(n_lev, 0)` above |
| Cook's distance | Combined effect of residual and leverage on the fit | $4/n$ = `r fmt(cook_cut, 4)` | `r fmt(n_cook, 0)` above; maximum `r fmt(max_cook, 3)` |
| DFBETA | Change in one coefficient when the observation is deleted | Context-dependent | — |

The picture is reassuring despite the counts. The proportion of standardised residuals beyond $\pm 2$ is `r fmt(100 * n_stdres / n_obs, 1)`%, almost exactly the 5% expected by chance under a correct model. More importantly, **the largest Cook's distance is `r fmt(max_cook, 3)`**, far below 1 and only a few multiples of the $4/n$ threshold. No single participant exerts material influence over the fitted model. This is a common and comfortable situation in large datasets: with `r fmt(n_obs, 0)` observations, no one record can dominate. In small studies the same diagnostics frequently identify one or two observations that change the conclusions entirely, which is why they should always be inspected. Observations flagged this way are candidates for **investigation**, never for automatic deletion.

## Tests for error normality {#sec-normality-tests}

Graphical assessment can be supplemented by formal tests. All share the same hypotheses:

$$
H_0: \text{the errors follow a normal distribution}
\qquad
H_A: \text{the errors do not follow a normal distribution}
$$

Note the direction: a **large** $p$-value is the favourable outcome, since it means the normality hypothesis is not rejected. Four tests are in common use.

| Test | Basis |
|:--------|:----------------------|
| **Anderson–Darling** | Measures the squared area between the empirical distribution of the residuals and the fitted normal cumulative distribution, weighted to give extra emphasis to the tails. Smaller $A^2$ indicates better agreement. |
| **Shapiro–Wilk** | Compares the ordered residuals with the values expected from a normal sample, forming a ratio $W$ that approaches 1 under normality. Small $W$ leads to rejection. |
| **Ryan–Joiner** | A simpler correlation-based alternative to Shapiro–Wilk: the correlation $R_p$ between the ordered residuals and their normal scores. Values near 1 indicate normality. |
| **Kolmogorov–Smirnov** (the **Lilliefors** test when parameters are estimated) | Takes the largest vertical distance $D$ between the empirical and the normal cumulative distribution functions. |

```{r}
#| label: normality-tests
res_mlr <- residuals(m_mlr)
sw   <- shapiro.test(res_mlr)
kstest <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(scale(res_mlr), "pnorm"))
```

Applied to the residuals of the multivariable model, the Shapiro–Wilk test gives $W$ = `r fmt(sw$statistic, 4)` with $p$ `r fmt_p(sw$p.value)`, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test gives $D$ = `r fmt(kstest$statistic, 4)` with $p$ `r fmt_p(kstest$p.value)`. Both reject normality decisively, agreeing with @fig-mlr-diagnostics.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Normality tests in large samples

These tests should not be given more weight than they deserve. Their power increases with sample size, so in large datasets they reject normality for departures far too small to affect any conclusion. With `r fmt(n_obs, 0)` observations, essentially no real dataset will pass. A significant result therefore establishes *that* the residuals are non-normal, but says nothing about *how much* it matters.

The practical rule is that **plots lead and tests corroborate**. Here the plots show substantial right skew, not a trivial departure, so the test result reflects something real. Had the normal probability plot looked straight, a significant Shapiro–Wilk test at this sample size would have warranted no action at all.

The consequences follow the sensitivity ordering of @sec-slr. Inference about the regression coefficients is fairly robust to non-normality, and at this sample size the central limit theorem makes the confidence intervals in @tbl-mlr broadly trustworthy on this count. Prediction intervals for individual participants are not robust and should not be used from this model.
:::

## Tests for constant error variance {#sec-variance-tests}

The second condition to be tested formally is equal variance. The hypotheses are

$$
H_0: \text{the error variance is constant}
\qquad
H_A: \text{the error variance is not constant}
$$

and again a large $p$-value is the favourable outcome. Several tests are available, most of which work by dividing the residuals into $g \ge 2$ groups — commonly by low versus high fitted values — and comparing variability between them.

| Test | Basis and requirements |
|:--------|:-----------------------|
| **F-test** | Splits residuals into two groups by predictor value and compares their variances directly through $F^* = s_1^2 / s_2^2$. Requires normal errors. |
| **Modified Levene**, also called the **Brown–Forsythe** test | Compares the mean absolute deviation of residuals from their **group median** across groups. Being based on medians it is nonparametric and **does not require normal errors**, which makes it the robust choice. |
| **Breusch–Pagan**, also called the **Cook–Weisberg score test** | Regresses the squared residuals on the predictors and tests whether that relationship is flat. Assumes normal errors. |
| **Bartlett's test** | Compares group variances through a pooled-variance statistic. Highly sensitive to non-normality; Levene's test is preferred when normality is in doubt. |

```{r}
#| label: variance-tests
bp <- bptest(m_mlr)
fit_grp <- cut(fitted(m_mlr), quantile(fitted(m_mlr), 0:4/4),
               include.lowest = TRUE, labels = paste("Q", 1:4))
lev <- car::leveneTest(residuals(m_mlr) ~ fit_grp, center = median)
grp_sd <- tibble(grp = fit_grp, r = residuals(m_mlr)) |>
  group_by(grp) |> summarise(sd = sd(r), .groups = "drop")
```

The **Breusch–Pagan** test gives $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(bp$statistic, 1)` on `r fmt(bp$parameter, 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ `r fmt_p(bp$p.value)`.

The **modified Levene (Brown–Forsythe)** test, dividing the residuals into quartiles of fitted value, gives $F$ = `r fmt(lev[1, "F value"], 1)` on `r fmt(lev[1, "Df"], 0)` and `r fmt(lev[2, "Df"], 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ `r fmt_p(lev[1, "Pr(>F)"])`.

Both reject the constant-variance hypothesis emphatically, and here the two tests reinforce one another usefully: Breusch–Pagan assumes normal errors, which has just been shown to fail, but Brown–Forsythe does not require normality and reaches the same conclusion. The failure is not an artefact of the normality violation.

The magnitude is easy to see directly. Residual standard deviations across quartiles of fitted value are `r paste(fmt(grp_sd$sd, 2), collapse = ", ")` mmol/L — the most variable quartile has roughly `r fmt(max(grp_sd$sd) / min(grp_sd$sd), 1)` times the spread of the least. This is a large departure, not a marginal one.

::: {.callout-important}
## What the diagnostics establish, and what follows

The multivariable model has **adequate linearity** for every predictor (@fig-mlr-resid-preds), **no influential observations** (@sec-assessing), and **no multicollinearity** (@sec-multicollinearity). Independence holds by design. But the errors are **not normally distributed** and, more seriously, their **variance is not constant**.

The practical consequence is specific. The coefficients in @tbl-mlr remain unbiased estimates — heteroscedasticity does not bias $b$. What is unreliable is their **precision**: the standard errors, and therefore the confidence intervals and $p$-values, are computed under an assumption the data contradict.

Two remedies are standard. The first is to **transform** a variable so that the conditions are better met, which is the subject of @sec-transformation. The second is to keep the model and compute **heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors**, which are valid without the equal-variance assumption. Both are legitimate; the first changes the model, the second changes only the inference drawn from it.
:::

# Transformation {#sec-transformation}

@sec-mlr-assessment left the multivariable model with two failed conditions. Transformation — re-expressing a predictor or the outcome on a different scale — is the classical remedy. Because a "linear" model requires linearity only in the parameters (@sec-mlr-model), a model fitted to transformed variables is still a linear model, and all the machinery of the preceding sections continues to apply.

This section covers when to transform a predictor, what other transformations are available, and what happens when they are applied to these data. The results are instructive precisely because they are mixed.

## Log-transforming a predictor {#sec-log-predictor}

The natural logarithm compresses large values and spreads out small ones. Applied to a predictor, it changes the *shape* of that predictor's relationship with the outcome without touching the outcome's error distribution.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When to consider log-transforming a predictor

Transforming a predictor is the appropriate first remedy when **non-linearity is the only problem** — when independence, normality and equal variance are already satisfactory. Specific indications are:

1. The **residuals-versus-predictor plot is curved**, with the outcome rising steeply at low predictor values and flattening at high ones.
2. The predictor is **strongly right-skewed**, so that a few large values exert disproportionate leverage.
3. The predictor plausibly acts **multiplicatively** rather than additively — that is, proportional rather than absolute changes are what matter biologically.
4. The predictor spans **several orders of magnitude**.
:::

Two constraints apply. The logarithm is undefined at zero and for negative values, so a strictly positive predictor is required. And transformation is **iterative**: conditions satisfied before a transformation may fail after it, so the diagnostics must be re-checked each time.

Interpretation changes in a way that must be handled carefully. With a predictor on the log scale, the coefficient is no longer a change per unit of the predictor but a change per *multiplicative* change. Using $\log_2$ rather than $\log_e$ makes this directly readable: **the coefficient becomes the change in mean outcome associated with a doubling of the predictor.**

### Application to fasting triglyceride

Among the continuous covariates in the model, fasting triglyceride is the most strongly right-skewed, with a skewness coefficient of `r fmt(mean(scale(na.omit(mssm$fasting_tg))^3), 2)` and values from `r fmt(min(mssm$fasting_tg, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$fasting_tg, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` mmol/L. It is also conventionally log-transformed in the lipid literature. It is therefore the natural candidate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tg-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of fasting triglyceride on the original and base-2 logarithmic scales. The log transformation converts a strongly right-skewed distribution into an approximately symmetric one, which is the usual motivation for applying it."
#| fig-height: 3.4

(ggplot(mssm |> filter(!is.na(fasting_tg)), aes(fasting_tg)) +
   geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey45") +
   labs(x = "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)", y = "Count", title = "Original scale")) +
(ggplot(mssm |> filter(!is.na(fasting_tg)), aes(log2(fasting_tg))) +
   geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey45") +
   labs(x = expression(log[2]*"(fasting triglyceride)"), y = "Count",
        title = "Base-2 log scale"))
```

@fig-tg-dist confirms that the transformation does what it is supposed to do to the predictor's own distribution. @tbl-log-tg compares the two models.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-log-tg
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of the multivariable model with fasting triglyceride entered untransformed and on a base-2 logarithmic scale. Only the triglyceride term differs between the models; all other covariates are as in @tbl-mlr."

tibble(
  Model = c("Triglyceride untransformed", "Triglyceride on log₂ scale"),
  `Triglyceride coefficient` = c(
    paste0(fmt(coef(m_mlr)["fasting_tg"], 3), " per mmol/L"),
    paste0(fmt(coef(m_log_tg)["log2(fasting_tg)"], 3), " per doubling")),
  `R²` = fmt(100 * c(summary(m_mlr)$r.squared, summary(m_log_tg)$r.squared), 2),
  `Adjusted R²` = fmt(100 * c(summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared,
                              summary(m_log_tg)$adj.r.squared), 2),
  `Residual SE` = fmt(c(sigma(m_mlr), sigma(m_log_tg)), 3),
  AIC = fmt(c(AIC(m_mlr), AIC(m_log_tg)), 1)
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88))
```

The coefficient on the log scale is `r b(m_log_tg, "log2(fasting_tg)", 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r ci(m_log_tg, "log2(fasting_tg)", 3)`), meaning that **a doubling of fasting triglyceride is associated with a mean fasting blood sugar higher by `r b(m_log_tg, "log2(fasting_tg)", 3)` mmol/L**, adjusted for the other covariates. That is an interpretable and clinically communicable statement.

::: {.callout-important}
## The transformation does not improve this model

Despite the strong skew that motivated it, log-transforming triglyceride makes the model slightly **worse**. Adjusted $R^2$ falls from `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared, 2)`% to `r fmt(100 * summary(m_log_tg)$adj.r.squared, 2)`%, the residual standard error rises from `r fmt(sigma(m_mlr), 3)` to `r fmt(sigma(m_log_tg), 3)` mmol/L, and AIC rises by `r fmt(AIC(m_log_tg) - AIC(m_mlr), 1)` points. On every criterion the untransformed model fits marginally better.

This is not a failure of the analysis but an illustration of an important principle. **A skewed predictor is not by itself a reason to transform.** The diagnostics in @fig-mlr-resid-preds showed that the linear specification of triglyceride was already adequate — the smoother was essentially flat. There was no non-linearity to fix, so the transformation had nothing to repair, and it slightly degraded a relationship that was already close to linear.

The rule that follows is: **transform in response to a diagnosed problem, not in response to a distribution.** Had these two models been compared only on $R^2$, with the transformation adopted or rejected on that basis, the reasoning would have been backwards. The choice between them here should rest on interpretability — and "per doubling" may well be preferable to "per mmol/L" for communicating to a clinical audience, at a negligible cost in fit.
:::

## Other transformations {#sec-other-transformations}

Log-transforming a predictor is one option among many. The main alternatives are summarised below.

| Transformation | Form | Typical use |
|:-----|:-------|:--------------------|
| Log of predictor | $\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x$ | Outcome rises steeply then flattens; right-skewed predictor |
| Log of outcome | $\mu_{\ln Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ | Right-skewed outcome; variance growing with the mean |
| Log of both | $\mu_{\ln Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x$ | Multiplicative relationships; coefficient becomes an elasticity |
| Reciprocal | $\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1/x)$ | Outcome approaching an asymptote |
| Exponential | $\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 e^{-x}$ | Decay relationships |
| Square root | $y^* = \sqrt{y}$ | Count outcomes; variance proportional to the mean |
| Arcsine | $\hat{p}^* = \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{\hat{p}})$ | Proportions (largely superseded by logistic regression) |
| Power / Box–Cox | $y^* = y^{\lambda}$ | General-purpose variance stabilisation, $\lambda$ estimated from the data |

Two of these deserve comment. The **square-root and arcsine transformations** were historically the standard treatment for counts and proportions, but Poisson and logistic regression now handle those outcomes directly and are usually preferable. The **Box–Cox procedure** provides a systematic way to select a power transformation of the outcome, estimating $\lambda$ by maximum likelihood over a range such as $[-2, 2]$; $\lambda = 1$ means no transformation, $\lambda = 0.5$ the square root, $\lambda = 0$ the logarithm, and $\lambda = -1$ the reciprocal. Values close to a recognisable transformation are conventionally rounded to it for interpretability.

Choosing among these remains partly trial and error. Two pieces of advice apply generally: **do not delete observations merely to make a transformation work**, and **prefer some loss of fit over the loss of a clearly interpretable model**, reporting the choice either way.

### Transforming the outcome

The diagnostics of @sec-mlr-assessment pointed to a problem with the *error distribution* rather than with any predictor's functional form: right-skewed residuals whose variance grows with the fitted value. That combination is the classic indication for transforming the **outcome**.

```{r}
#| label: boxcox
bc <- MASS::boxcox(m_mlr, lambda = seq(-2, 2, 0.05), plotit = FALSE)
lambda_hat <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
```

The Box–Cox procedure applied to this model estimates $\hat{\lambda}$ = `r fmt(lambda_hat, 2)`, close enough to zero to justify the logarithmic transformation, which is also the more interpretable choice. @tbl-log-fbs and @fig-log-fbs-diag compare the models before and after.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-log-fbs
#| tbl-cap: "The multivariable model with fasting blood sugar untransformed and log-transformed. R² values are not directly comparable between the two models because the outcomes are on different scales; the diagnostic quantities are."

bp_log <- bptest(m_log_fbs)
sw_log <- shapiro.test(residuals(m_log_fbs))

tibble(
  Quantity = c("Adjusted R²  (%)", "Residual skewness", "Shapiro–Wilk W",
               "Breusch–Pagan χ²", "Breusch–Pagan p"),
  `Outcome untransformed` = c(
    fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared, 2),
    fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_mlr))^3), 2),
    fmt(sw$statistic, 3),
    fmt(bp$statistic, 1),
    fmt_p(bp$p.value)),
  `Outcome log-transformed` = c(
    fmt(100 * summary(m_log_fbs)$adj.r.squared, 2),
    fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_log_fbs))^3), 2),
    fmt(sw_log$statistic, 3),
    fmt(bp_log$statistic, 1),
    fmt_p(bp_log$p.value))
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-fbs-diag
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic plots before and after log-transforming the outcome. The top row is the original model, the bottom row the log-transformed model. The transformation substantially improves the symmetry of the residuals and reduces, but does not remove, the fan shape in the residuals-versus-fitted plot."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

(p_resid_fit(m_mlr, "Original outcome: residuals vs fitted") |
   p_qq(m_mlr, "Original outcome: normal probability plot")) /
((p_resid_fit(m_log_fbs, "Log outcome: residuals vs fitted") +
    labs(x = "Fitted value (log mmol/L)", y = "Residual (log scale)")) |
   p_qq(m_log_fbs, "Log outcome: normal probability plot"))
```

The improvement in the residual distribution is substantial. Residual skewness falls from `r fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_mlr))^3), 2)` to `r fmt(mean(scale(residuals(m_log_fbs))^3), 2)`, and the Shapiro–Wilk statistic rises from `r fmt(sw$statistic, 3)` to `r fmt(sw_log$statistic, 3)`. The normal probability plot in @fig-log-fbs-diag is far closer to a straight line, and adjusted $R^2$ on the log scale is `r fmt(100 * summary(m_log_fbs)$adj.r.squared, 1)`%.

::: {.callout-important}
## The transformation helps substantially but does not fix the problem

Both formal tests still reject decisively: Shapiro–Wilk $p$ `r fmt_p(sw_log$p.value)` and Breusch–Pagan $p$ `r fmt_p(bp_log$p.value)`. @fig-log-fbs-diag shows why — the residual spread still widens with the fitted value, less dramatically than before but visibly.

It would be easy, and wrong, to present the log transformation as having solved the problem. It has improved matters considerably and has not resolved them. Reporting a transformed model without re-examining its diagnostics is a common error, and it is precisely the iterative re-checking urged in @sec-log-predictor that catches it.

Where does that leave the analysis? Three defensible positions, in increasing order of effort:

1. **Keep the untransformed model and use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors.** The coefficients keep their direct mmol/L interpretation, and the inference no longer depends on the equal-variance assumption.
2. **Use the log-transformed model**, accepting the change of interpretation and the residual imperfection, and report the diagnostics honestly.
3. **Use a model designed for a skewed positive outcome**, such as a gamma regression with a log link, which specifies a mean–variance relationship appropriate to the data rather than requiring a transformation to manufacture one.
:::

Interpretation on the log scale is worth stating explicitly, since it changes from additive to multiplicative. Exponentiating a coefficient converts it into a ratio of geometric means. For history of diabetes, the coefficient of `r fmt(coef(m_log_fbs)["hx_dm2Yes"], 3)` gives $e^{`r fmt(coef(m_log_fbs)["hx_dm2Yes"], 3)`}$ = `r fmt(exp(coef(m_log_fbs)["hx_dm2Yes"]), 3)`, so participants with a diabetes history have a geometric mean fasting blood sugar about `r fmt(100 * (exp(coef(m_log_fbs)["hx_dm2Yes"]) - 1), 0)`% higher than those without, adjusted for the other covariates. Note that back-transforming the fitted values by exponentiating gives geometric rather than arithmetic means, which are systematically lower; this is a well-known trap when predictions are required on the original scale.

## Generalized additive models {#sec-gam}

Transformation addresses non-linearity by requiring the analyst to *choose* a functional form — a logarithm, a square root, a reciprocal — and then imposing it. **Generalized additive models (GAMs)** take a different approach: they let the data determine the shape.

A GAM replaces the linear term $\beta_j x_j$ with a smooth function $f_j(x_j)$ estimated from the data:

$$
g\left( E\{Y\} \right) = \beta_0 + f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k)
$$

where $g$ is a link function, equal to the identity for a continuous outcome of the kind modelled in this chapter. Each $f_j$ is typically built from splines, and its wiggliness is controlled by a penalty chosen automatically, usually by cross-validation or restricted maximum likelihood. A linear term is a special case: where the data support a straight line, the fitted smooth *is* a straight line.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Strengths of GAMs over multiple linear regression

1. **The shape of the exposure–outcome relationship is estimated, not assumed.** This matters in epidemiology, where dose–response shape is often the scientific question.
2. **Continuous exposures need not be categorised.** Splitting a continuous variable into quartiles to accommodate non-linearity discards information and reduces power; a smooth term avoids the compromise entirely.
3. **Non-monotone and threshold relationships can be captured** — J-shaped and U-shaped associations, common for blood pressure, body mass index and many biomarkers, which no single transformation represents well.
4. **The degree of smoothing is chosen by the fitting procedure**, through a penalty on wiggliness, rather than by the analyst inspecting plots and choosing a polynomial degree.
5. **Additivity is retained**, so each covariate's contribution can still be examined and plotted one at a time. A GAM is far more interpretable than a fully non-parametric model.
:::

The costs should be stated as plainly as the benefits. There is **no single coefficient to report** for a smoothed covariate — the result is a curve, conveyed by a plot and an effective-degrees-of-freedom value, which is harder to tabulate and to communicate to non-statistical audiences. Flexible models can **overfit**, following features of the sample that will not replicate. And where a linear term is adequate, as @fig-mlr-resid-preds indicates is the case for every predictor in this chapter's model, a GAM adds complexity without adding insight.

In R, GAMs are fitted with the `gam()` function of the **mgcv** package, using terms of the form `s(age)` to request a smooth. Readers whose diagnostics show genuine curvature that no simple transformation resolves should regard GAMs as the natural next step.

# Interaction {#sec-interaction}

Every model fitted so far has made an assumption so quietly that it has not yet been stated: that each covariate's association with fasting blood sugar is the same for everyone. The coefficient for age in @tbl-mlr is a single number, applied identically to men and women, to rural and urban participants, and to those with and without diabetes. This section examines that assumption, and shows that in these data it is wrong.

## Additive effects {#sec-additive}

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: additive effects

Two predictors have **additive effects** when the response function can be written as a sum of separate functions of each predictor:

$$
\mu_Y = f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k)
$$

The effect of each predictor on the mean outcome is then the same regardless of the values taken by the others.
:::

The first-order model $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i$ is additive by construction. Its geometry is best seen with one continuous and one binary predictor. Writing $x_2 = 0$ and $x_2 = 1$ for the two groups:

$$
\text{Group } x_2 = 0: \quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1
$$
$$
\text{Group } x_2 = 1: \quad \mu_Y = (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + \beta_1 x_1
$$

The two lines have **the same slope** $\beta_1$ and differ only in their intercepts, by the constant amount $\beta_2$.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The visual signature of additivity is parallel lines

Under an additive model, the fitted lines for different groups are exactly parallel. The vertical distance between them, $\beta_2$, is constant at every value of $x_1$ — so a single number describes the group difference, and a single slope describes the effect of $x_1$ in both groups.
:::

@fig-additive shows what the additive model of @tbl-mlr implies for the relationship between age and fasting blood sugar in participants with and without a history of diabetes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-additive
#| fig-cap: "Predicted fasting blood sugar by age and history of diabetes, as implied by the additive multivariable model of @tbl-mlr. The two fitted lines are exactly parallel by construction: the model permits the groups to differ in level but forces them to share a single age slope. Predictions are averaged over the other covariates."
#| fig-height: 3.8

emmip(m_mlr, hx_dm2 ~ age, at = list(age = seq(20, 85, length.out = 30)),
      CIs = TRUE, plotit = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)",
       colour = "History of diabetes", fill = "History of diabetes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The parallelism in @fig-additive is not a finding. It is an **assumption**, imposed by a model that contains no term permitting the slopes to differ. Whether the data support it is a separate question.

## Multiplicative effects and interaction {#sec-interaction-concept}

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition: interaction

Two predictors **interact** when the effect of one on the outcome depends on the value of the other. Equivalently, the response function is **not additive** — it cannot be written as a sum of separate functions of each predictor:

$$
\mu_Y \ne f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k)
$$
:::

Interaction is introduced into a linear model by including the **product** of the two predictors as an additional term:

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i
$$

The product $x_{i1} x_{i2}$ is the **two-way interaction term**. The model remains a linear model — setting $x_{i3} = x_{i1}x_{i2}$ recovers the standard three-predictor form — which is why interaction requires no new estimation theory.

To see what the product term does, separate the group-specific equations as before:

$$
\text{Group } x_2 = 0: \quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1
$$
$$
\text{Group } x_2 = 1: \quad \mu_Y = (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + (\beta_1 + \beta_3) x_1
$$

Now the lines differ in **both** intercept and slope. The interaction coefficient $\beta_3$ is precisely the **difference between the two groups' slopes**. Non-parallel lines are the visual signature of interaction, exactly as parallel lines are the signature of additivity.

The same logic applies when both predictors are continuous. For $E\{Y\} = 10 + 2x_1 + 5x_2 + 0.5 x_1 x_2$, the slope with respect to $x_1$ is $2 + 0.5x_2$, which depends on $x_2$. At $x_2 = 1$ the relationship is $E\{Y\} = 15 + 2.5x_1$; at $x_2 = 3$ it is $E\{Y\} = 25 + 3.5x_1$. Rather than two lines, the fitted surface becomes a twisted plane.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Three rules for models containing interaction

**1. Main effects change meaning.** With $x_1x_2$ in the model, $\beta_1$ is no longer "the effect of $x_1$". It is the effect of $x_1$ **when $x_2 = 0$** — a conditional effect at one specific value. If $x_2 = 0$ is outside the observed range, $\beta_1$ may have no interpretable meaning at all. Centring continuous predictors before forming their product makes the main effects interpretable at average values and is standard practice.

**2. Respect the hierarchy principle.** If an interaction term is included, both of its component main effects should be retained, **whether or not they are individually significant**. Omitting a main effect while keeping the product imposes a constraint that is rarely intended.

**3. Prefer one F-test to several t-tests.** When several interaction terms are assessed together, a single general linear F-test (@sec-f-test) is preferable to a series of individual $t$-tests, because each additional test inflates the overall error rate.
:::

Epidemiologists will recognise interaction under other names. **Effect modification** and **moderation** describe the same statistical phenomenon: a third variable that alters the strength or direction of an exposure–outcome association. A moderator is distinct from a confounder or a mediator, both discussed in @sec-crude-adjusted — a confounder biases an estimate, a mediator transmits it, and a moderator changes it depending on who you are.

## Interaction between two numerical covariates {#sec-int-cont}

The multivariable model contains six continuous covariates, and any pair might interact. Three plausible pairs were specified for testing before any were fitted, each motivated by the metabolic syndrome hypothesis that adiposity and dyslipidaemia act together rather than separately. Each was added in turn to the model of @tbl-mlr and assessed with a general linear F-test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-int-search
#| tbl-cap: "Three candidate numerical-by-numerical interactions, each added in turn to the multivariable model and tested against it with a general linear F-test. The pairs were specified in this order before fitting."

int_search |>
  mutate(
    `F` = fmt(f, 2),
    `p-value` = if_else(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p, 4)),
    Conclusion = if_else(p < 0.05, "Evidence of interaction", "No evidence")
  ) |>
  select(Pair = pair, `F`, `p-value`, Conclusion) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(88))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Disclosure of the search

Three interactions were examined and two reached conventional significance. The strongest, **waist–hip ratio by fasting triglyceride**, is presented in detail below. This search is reported because it affects interpretation: a $p$-value obtained after three tests is weaker evidence than the same value from a single pre-specified hypothesis. A Bonferroni adjustment across the three tests would require $p < 0.017$, which this result meets comfortably at $p$ = `r fmt(int_search$p[3], 5)`. An interaction identified in this way should nonetheless be described as **exploratory** and reported together with the search that produced it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-int-cont
#| tbl-cap: "Multivariable model with an added interaction between waist-hip ratio and fasting triglyceride. Only the terms involved in the interaction are shown; the remaining covariates are as in @tbl-mlr."

anova_cont <- anova(m_mlr, m_int_cont)

tidy(m_int_cont, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term %in% c("whr", "fasting_tg", tm_cont)) |>
  mutate(Term = case_when(term == "whr" ~ "Waist-hip ratio",
                          term == "fasting_tg" ~ "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)",
                          TRUE ~ "Waist-hip ratio x triglyceride"),
         b = fmt(estimate, 5),
         CI = paste0(fmt(conf.low, 5), " to ", fmt(conf.high, 5)),
         p = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p.value, 4))) |>
  select(Term, b, `95% CI` = CI, p) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

The interaction coefficient is `r b(m_int_cont, tm_cont, 4)` (95% CI `r ci(m_int_cont, tm_cont, 4)`), and the general linear F-test comparing this model with the additive model gives $F$ = `r fmt(anova_cont$F[2], 2)` on 1 and `r fmt(anova_cont$Res.Df[2], 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ = `r fmt(anova_cont[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 5)`.

The positive sign means the two covariates' effects are **super-additive**: the association between triglyceride and fasting blood sugar becomes *stronger* as central adiposity increases. Because the interaction coefficient is the amount by which the triglyceride slope changes per one-unit increase in waist–hip ratio, the slope at any given WHR is obtained by substitution:

$$
\text{slope of triglyceride at WHR } w = `r fmt(coef(m_int_cont)["fasting_tg"], 4)` + (`r fmt(coef(m_int_cont)[tm_cont], 4)` \times w)
$$

```{r}
#| label: slopes-cont
slope_at <- function(w) coef(m_int_cont)["fasting_tg"] +
  coef(m_int_cont)[tm_cont] * w
whr_q <- quantile(mssm$whr, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
```

At the lower quartile of waist–hip ratio (`r fmt(whr_q[1], 2)`) the triglyceride slope is `r fmt(slope_at(whr_q[1]), 3)` mmol/L per mmol/L; at the median (`r fmt(whr_q[2], 2)`) it is `r fmt(slope_at(whr_q[2]), 3)`; and at the upper quartile (`r fmt(whr_q[3], 2)`) it is `r fmt(slope_at(whr_q[3]), 3)`. Across the interquartile range of central adiposity, in other words, the strength of the triglyceride–glycaemia association increases by roughly `r fmt(100 * (slope_at(whr_q[3]) / slope_at(whr_q[1]) - 1), 0)`%. @fig-int-cont displays this.

```{r}
#| label: fig-int-cont
#| fig-cap: "Predicted fasting blood sugar against fasting triglyceride at the quartiles of waist-hip ratio, from the model containing their interaction. The lines are not parallel: the triglyceride slope steepens as central adiposity increases, so the two exposures reinforce one another."
#| fig-height: 3.8

emmip(m_int_cont, whr ~ fasting_tg,
      at = list(whr = as.numeric(round(whr_q, 2)),
                fasting_tg = seq(0.5, 6, length.out = 30)),
      CIs = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fasting triglyceride (mmol/L)",
       y = "Predicted fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)",
       colour = "Waist-hip ratio", fill = "Waist-hip ratio") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The finding is biologically coherent: central obesity and hypertriglyceridaemia are both components of the metabolic syndrome, and the model suggests their effects on fasting glucose compound rather than merely add. Two observations nonetheless temper it. The main effects in @tbl-int-cont are now negative and statistically significant, which looks alarming until one recalls rule 1 below — each is the effect of one variable when the *other* is zero, and neither zero triglyceride nor zero waist–hip ratio exists. And the gain in explanatory power is slight: adjusted $R^2$ rises from `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mlr)$adj.r.squared, 2)`% to `r fmt(100 * summary(m_int_cont)$adj.r.squared, 2)`%. **The interaction is real and interpretable, but it refines the model rather than transforming it.**

## Interaction between a numerical and a categorical covariate {#sec-int-cat}

The second interaction was specified in advance rather than discovered: between **age** and **history of diabetes**. It is the more instructive of the two.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-int-cat
#| tbl-cap: "Multivariable model with an added interaction between age and history of diabetes. Only the terms involved in the interaction are shown; the remaining covariates are as in @tbl-mlr."

anova_cat <- anova(m_mlr, m_int_cat)

tidy(m_int_cat, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term %in% c("age", "hx_dm2Yes", "age:hx_dm2Yes")) |>
  mutate(Term = c("Age (years)", "History of diabetes (yes vs no)",
                  "Age x diabetes history")[
                    match(term, c("age", "hx_dm2Yes", "age:hx_dm2Yes"))],
         b = fmt(estimate, 5),
         CI = paste0(fmt(conf.low, 5), " to ", fmt(conf.high, 5)),
         p = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p.value, 4))) |>
  select(Term, b, `95% CI` = CI, p) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

The interaction coefficient is `r b(m_int_cat, "age:hx_dm2Yes", 4)` (95% CI `r ci(m_int_cat, "age:hx_dm2Yes", 4)`), and the general linear F-test gives $F$ = `r fmt(anova_cat$F[2], 2)` on 1 and `r fmt(anova_cat$Res.Df[2], 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ `r fmt_p(anova_cat[["Pr(>F)"]][2])`. This is strong evidence against the additive model.

### Recovering the two age slopes

The interaction coefficient is the *difference* between slopes, so each group's slope is obtained by substitution:

```{r}
#| label: slopes-cat
sl_no  <- coef(m_int_cat)["age"]
sl_yes <- coef(m_int_cat)["age"] + coef(m_int_cat)["age:hx_dm2Yes"]
emt <- emtrends(m_int_cat, ~ hx_dm2, var = "age") |> as_tibble()
```

$$
\text{No diabetes history:} \quad \text{slope} = `r fmt(sl_no, 5)` \ \text{mmol/L per year}
$$
$$
\text{Diabetes history:} \quad \text{slope} = `r fmt(sl_no, 5)` + (`r fmt(coef(m_int_cat)["age:hx_dm2Yes"], 5)`) = `r fmt(sl_yes, 5)` \ \text{mmol/L per year}
$$

@tbl-emtrends confirms these with their confidence intervals, computed as estimated marginal trends.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-emtrends
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated slope of fasting blood sugar on age, separately by history of diabetes, from the interaction model. The two slopes have opposite signs and their confidence intervals do not overlap."

emt |>
  mutate(Group = paste("History of diabetes:", hx_dm2),
         Slope = fmt(age.trend, 5),
         CI = paste0(fmt(lower.CL, 5), " to ", fmt(upper.CL, 5))) |>
  select(Group, `Slope (mmol/L per year)` = Slope, `95% CI` = CI) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(90))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The two groups behave in opposite directions

Among participants **without** a history of diabetes, fasting blood sugar rises with age by `r fmt(sl_no, 4)` mmol/L per year — roughly `r fmt(10 * sl_no, 2)` mmol/L per decade, a small but positive gradient consistent with the gradual decline in glucose tolerance expected with ageing.

Among participants **with** a history of diabetes, fasting blood sugar **falls** with age, by `r fmt(abs(sl_yes), 4)` mmol/L per year, or about `r fmt(abs(10 * sl_yes), 2)` mmol/L per decade.

The additive model of @tbl-mlr, forced to fit a single slope to both groups, returned `r b(m_mlr, "age", 4)` mmol/L per year and no evidence of any age association at all. It arrived at that null result by averaging two real and opposing gradients.
:::

@fig-int-cat shows the two fitted relationships.

```{r}
#| label: fig-int-cat
#| fig-cap: "Predicted fasting blood sugar by age and history of diabetes, from the model containing their interaction. Compare with @fig-additive, where the same two lines were constrained to be parallel. Here they converge sharply: among those without a diabetes history the line rises gently, while among those with one it falls. Shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-height: 4

emmip(m_int_cat, hx_dm2 ~ age, at = list(age = seq(20, 85, length.out = 30)),
      CIs = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted fasting blood sugar (mmol/L)",
       colour = "History of diabetes", fill = "History of diabetes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: emm-ages
emm_ages <- emmeans(m_int_cat, ~ age | hx_dm2,
                    at = list(age = c(30, 50, 70))) |> as_tibble()
get_emm <- function(a, g) {
  emm_ages$emmean[emm_ages$age == a & emm_ages$hx_dm2 == g]
}
```

The gap between the groups narrows markedly across the age range. At age 30 the adjusted mean fasting blood sugar is `r fmt(get_emm(30, "No"), 2)` mmol/L without a diabetes history and `r fmt(get_emm(30, "Yes"), 2)` mmol/L with one, a difference of `r fmt(get_emm(30, "Yes") - get_emm(30, "No"), 2)` mmol/L. By age 70 the corresponding means are `r fmt(get_emm(70, "No"), 2)` and `r fmt(get_emm(70, "Yes"), 2)` mmol/L, a difference of only `r fmt(get_emm(70, "Yes") - get_emm(70, "No"), 2)` mmol/L.

### Interpreting the finding

A statistical result of this kind invites explanation, and explanation should be clearly separated from evidence. A plausible reading is that younger people with diagnosed diabetes represent a more severe phenotype — earlier onset, often poorer glycaemic control — whereas older people with a diabetes diagnosis include many with milder, later-onset disease detected through screening and managed for years with treatment. Survivor effects may contribute, since those with the worst control may not survive to older ages. **This is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a finding of this analysis.** The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish among these explanations, and nothing in the model tests them.

What the analysis does establish is methodological, and it is the central lesson of this section.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reporting practice when interaction is present

1. **Report stratum-specific effects, not a single adjusted coefficient.** Once interaction is established, "the effect of age" does not exist as a single quantity. Report `r fmt(sl_no, 4)` mmol/L per year for those without a diabetes history and `r fmt(sl_yes, 4)` for those with one, each with its confidence interval.
2. **Do not interpret the main effects in the usual way.** In @tbl-int-cat the coefficient for diabetes history, `r b(m_int_cat, "hx_dm2Yes", 3)`, is the group difference **at age zero** — an extrapolation far outside the observed range of `r fmt(min(mssm$age, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` to `r fmt(max(mssm$age, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` years, and not a meaningful quantity.
3. **Test interaction deliberately, and only where there is reason to.** Every pair of covariates could be multiplied together; testing them all guarantees spurious findings. Pre-specify the interactions that subject-matter knowledge suggests, and disclose any search, as was done in @sec-int-cont.
4. **Remember that interaction is scale-dependent.** Two variables that interact on the additive scale used here may not interact on a multiplicative scale, and vice versa. A statement about interaction is always a statement about a particular scale of measurement.
:::

The contrast between @fig-additive and @fig-int-cat is the strongest argument in this chapter for checking assumptions rather than accepting them. The additive model was not obviously deficient: its diagnostics were no worse than any other model here, and its age coefficient was reported with a respectable standard error. It was nonetheless concealing two opposing relationships behind a single null result.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This chapter developed linear regression from a single predictor to a multivariable model with interaction, checking the model's assumptions at each stage and applying every technique to the same outcome in the same dataset. Six learning points summarise what that exercise established. Each is drawn from a result the chapter actually produced, and each is stated as guidance for the reader's own analyses.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Six learning points

**1. Statistical significance and explanatory power are different things, and large samples separate them completely.**

In @sec-slr, `r fmt(n_sig, 0)` of `r n_cov` covariates were significantly associated with fasting blood sugar, yet apart from history of diabetes none explained more than `r fmt(100 * r2_next, 1)`% of its variance. Marital status achieved $p$ = `r fmt(summary(m_mar)$coefficients["maritalSingle", 4], 4)` while explaining `r fmt(100 * summary(m_mar)$r.squared, 2)`% of the variation — about one part in `r fmt(round(1 / summary(m_mar)$r.squared), 0)`. With several thousand observations, a $p$-value establishes only that an association is not zero; it says nothing about whether the association matters. Report the effect size with its confidence interval, let $R^2$ describe explanatory power, and let neither substitute for the other.

**2. The regression equation is the deliverable, and interpretation follows from it mechanically.**

Writing out the fitted equation with its units makes interpretation almost automatic, for continuous and categorical predictors alike. A slope of `r b(m_bmi, "bmi")` mmol/L per kg/m² becomes the more communicable `r fmt(5 * coef(m_bmi)["bmi"], 3)` mmol/L per 5 kg/m²; and for an indicator variable, the intercept is the reference group's mean while the coefficient is the difference between groups, as @sec-worked-categorical verified against the directly computed means. Rescale a coefficient whenever its natural unit is much smaller or larger than the spread of the variable — the waist–hip ratio coefficient in @sec-mlr-fit is the clearest case. Keep the units attached, state the direction, and check that the intercept is meaningful before interpreting it — at a body mass index of zero, it is not.

**3. Fit the model, then look at the residuals — and let the plots lead the tests.**

Both simple models in @sec-slr-assessment produced entirely respectable coefficient tables, and both had markedly skewed residuals — the body mass index model with non-constant variance as well. A coefficient table looks identical whether the assumptions hold or fail. Note too that the two models failed differently: the marital status model passed the constant-variance check that the body mass index model failed, so assumptions must be checked for the model actually fitted rather than assumed to carry over from another model of the same outcome. Residuals-versus-fitted plots reveal non-constant variance and non-linearity, normal probability plots reveal skew, and residuals plotted against omitted predictors reveal what the model has left out — as @fig-bmi-resid-others did, arguing for a multivariable model on evidence rather than assertion. Formal tests corroborate what the plots show; at these sample sizes they reject essentially any real data, so a significant Shapiro–Wilk result is informative only when the plot agrees.

**4. Adjustment can overturn a crude result, and only subject-matter knowledge decides which result answers the question.**

The clearest finding in this chapter is that age, strongly associated with fasting blood sugar when examined alone (`r fmt(crude_tab$crude[crude_tab$term == "age"], 4)` mmol/L per year, $p$ = `r fmt_psci(crude_tab$crude_p[crude_tab$term == "age"])`), showed no association whatever after adjustment (`r b(m_mlr, "age", 4)` mmol/L per year, $p$ = `r fmt_p(summary(m_mlr)$coefficients["age", 4])`). Adjustment removed a real association because the covariates transmitting it — body mass index, blood pressure, diabetes status — are plausibly consequences of ageing rather than confounders of it. Confounders and mediators are statistically indistinguishable; both change the coefficient. Always report crude and adjusted estimates side by side, and justify the covariate set on causal reasoning rather than on which variables happen to be significant.

**5. Test groups of parameters with the general linear F-test, and check the assumptions that individual coefficients cannot reveal.**

Ethnicity occupies three coefficients in the model, one of which is not significant. Reading them individually gives no answer to "does ethnicity matter?"; the general linear F-test does, giving $F$ = `r fmt(f_race, 2)` on `r fmt(df_r - df_f, 0)` and `r fmt(df_f, 0)` degrees of freedom, $p$ < 0.001 (@sec-f-test). One test is also safer than three, and unlike the individual contrasts it does not depend on the choice of reference category. Two further problems are invisible in a coefficient table read on its own. @sec-mlr-assessment showed the model failing the constant-variance condition emphatically (Breusch–Pagan $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(bp$statistic, 0)`, $p$ < 0.001), which leaves the coefficients unbiased but their standard errors unreliable. And @sec-collinearity-demo showed that adding waist circumference to a model already containing body mass index and waist–hip ratio drove all three adiposity terms to non-significance while improving the fit not at all — a model can appear to show that adiposity does not matter simply because it has been asked to measure it three times.

**6. Check whether effects are additive before reporting a single adjusted coefficient.**

Every model before @sec-interaction assumed each covariate acts identically for everyone. For age that assumption was wrong. Allowing the age slope to differ by diabetes history gave `r fmt(sl_no, 4)` mmol/L per year among participants without a history and `r fmt(sl_yes, 4)` among those with one — gradients of opposite sign, with an interaction test of $F$ = `r fmt(anova_cat$F[2], 1)`, $p$ < 0.001. The additive model's null age coefficient was the average of two real and opposing relationships. Once interaction is established, report stratum-specific effects rather than a single slope, do not interpret main effects in the usual way, and pre-specify the interactions worth testing — disclosing any search, as @sec-int-cont does.
:::

## Closing remarks

Two themes run through these points. The first is that **the model's output is never self-validating**. Coefficients, standard errors and $p$-values are produced identically whether the assumptions hold or fail, whether a crucial covariate is omitted, and whether an effect is uniform or reverses direction between subgroups. Everything of value in a regression analysis comes from what the analyst does after the model is fitted.

The second is that **statistics cannot supply the subject-matter reasoning it depends on**. Whether to adjust for a variable, whether an association is worth reporting, whether an interaction is plausible or an artefact of searching, and whether any of it supports a causal claim are questions that regression poses but cannot answer. The techniques in this chapter make those questions precise and quantify what the data say about them. Answering them remains the responsibility of the researcher.

Readers ready to go further will find the natural extensions close at hand. Logistic regression handles binary outcomes, Poisson and negative binomial regression handle counts, Cox regression handles time to event, and mixed-effects models handle grouped or repeated measurements. Each relaxes one assumption of the model developed here while retaining its structure, its vocabulary and its diagnostic logic. The effort invested in understanding linear regression thoroughly is repaid in all of them.

## Dataset

The **Metabolic Syndrome Study for Malaysia (MSSM)** dataset used throughout this chapter is a community-based health survey of `r fmt(n_total, 0)` adults, held by the author. It is used here for teaching purposes. Body mass index and waist–hip ratio were derived from the recorded weight, height, waist circumference and hip circumference as described in @sec-derived; all other variables are as collected.
